metadata.title: A Local converse theorem for Archimedean $\GL(n)$

extraction_notes.note: The label E:GL(2)xGL(2)_ep is defined twice (equations (2.14) and (2.16)); no \ref uses it, so no edge is affected.
Sections 4 and 5 are proofs without a proof environment filling whole sections; each is one proof node whose subsections Step 1-3 are its labelled steps.
Sharpness claims announced in the introduction and Section 6 opening were not made nodes; the formal claims before Examples 1 and 2 carry them.
Classification of Weil-group representations is stated in prose as background from Tate; kept as external claims rather than theorems because the paper names no result.

nodes.name: Henniart's local converse theorem
nodes.statement: If $F$ is non-archimedean, the first major result is the one by Henniart (\cite{Henniart1}) in which he shows that if two {\it generic} representations $\pi, \pi'\in\operatorname{Irr}_n$ are such that \[ \gamma(s, \pi\otimes\tau, \psi)=\gamma(s, \pi'\otimes\tau, \psi) \] for all $\tau\in\operatorname{Irr}_t$ for all $t=1,\dots,n-1$, where the $\gamma$-factor is the one defined by Jacquet, Piatetski-Shapiro and Shalika, then $\pi=\pi'$.
nodes.statement_short: For non-archimedean $F$, generic $\pi,\pi'$ with equal JPSS $\gamma$-factors under all $\operatorname{GL}_t$-twists, $t\le n-1$, are equal.
assumptions: two {\it generic} representations $\pi, \pi'\in\operatorname{Irr}_n$ are such that \[ \gamma(s, \pi\otimes\tau, \psi)=\gamma(s, \pi'\otimes\tau, \psi) \] for all $\tau\in\operatorname{Irr}_t$ for all $t=1,\dots,n-1$

nodes.name: Chen's n x (n-2) local converse theorem
nodes.statement: Later, in \cite{Chen} Chen improved this result by requiring $t$ be only up to $n-2$ with the extra assumption that $\pi$ and $\pi'$ have the same central character (we note that it was later known that $\operatorname{GL}_1$ twisting determines the central character; see, for example, \cite{JNS}).
nodes.statement_short: Henniart's theorem holds with twists only up to $t\le n-2$ when $\pi,\pi'$ have the same central character.

nodes.name: Jacquet's conjecture on the local converse problem
nodes.statement: It had been conjectured by Jacquet for some time that one only needs $t\leq[\frac{n}{2}]$.
nodes.origin_citation: Jacquet (as reported via Chai; Jacquet & Liu)
nodes.statement_short: Twists up to $t\le[n/2]$ suffice in the local converse theorem.

nodes.name: Jacquet's conjecture (Chai; Jacquet-Liu)
nodes.statement: And very recently this conjecture has been proven by Chai in \cite{Chai}, and Jacquet and Liu in \cite{JL} (see also \cite{ALSX, JNS}).

nodes.name: Local converse theorem for GL_n(C)
nodes.statement: Let $F=\mathbb C$. If the two representations $\pi, \pi'\in\operatorname{Irr}_n$ of $\operatorname{GL}_n(\mathbb C)$ satisfy \[ L(s, \pi\times\chi)=L(s, \pi'\times\chi) \] for all characters $\chi$ on $\mathbb C^\times$, where the $L$-factors are of Artin type defined by the local Langlands correspondence, then $\pi=\pi'$.
nodes.statement_short: Over $\mathbb C$, equality of Artin-type $L$-factors under all $\operatorname{GL}(1)$-twists determines $\pi\in\operatorname{Irr}_n$.
assumptions: the two representations $\pi, \pi'\in\operatorname{Irr}_n$ of $\operatorname{GL}_n(\mathbb C)$ satisfy \[ L(s, \pi\times\chi)=L(s, \pi'\times\chi) \] for all characters $\chi$ on $\mathbb C^\times$

nodes.name: Local converse theorem for GL_n(R)
nodes.statement: Let $F=\mathbb{R}$. If the two representations $\pi, \pi'\in\operatorname{Irr}_n$ of $\operatorname{GL}_n(\mathbb{R})$ satisfy \[ L(s, \pi\times\tau)=L(s, \pi'\times\tau) \] for all $\tau\in\operatorname{Irr}_t$ with $t=1, 2$, where the $L$-factors are of Artin type defined by the local Langlands correspondence, then $\pi=\pi'$.
nodes.statement_short: Over $\mathbb R$, equality of Artin-type $L$-factors under all $\operatorname{GL}(1)$- and $\operatorname{GL}(2)$-twists determines $\pi\in\operatorname{Irr}_n$.
assumptions: the two representations $\pi, \pi'\in\operatorname{Irr}_n$ of $\operatorname{GL}_n(\mathbb{R})$ satisfy \[ L(s, \pi\times\tau)=L(s, \pi'\times\tau) \] for all $\tau\in\operatorname{Irr}_t$ with $t=1, 2$

nodes.name: Base field F
nodes.statement: Throughout, $F$ is either $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb C$.

nodes.name: Irr_n
nodes.statement: We let $\operatorname{Irr}_n$ be the set of infinitesimal equivalence classes of irreducible admissible representations of $\operatorname{GL}_n(F)$.
also_stated_at: Let $F$ be a local field of characteristic 0, and let $\operatorname{Irr}_n$ be the set of (infinitesimal) equivalence classes of irreducible admissible representations of $\operatorname{GL}_n(F)$.

nodes.name: Absolute value |z|
nodes.statement: For $z\in F$, we let $|z|=\sqrt{z\bar{z}}$, so that if $F=\mathbb{R}$, this is the absolute value of $z$, and if $F=\mathbb C$, it is the usual modulus of $z$.

nodes.name: Norm ||z||
nodes.statement: We also let $\|z\|=z\bar{z}=|z|^2$.

nodes.name: Character (quasi-character)
nodes.statement: By a character, we always mean a quasi-character, and $\operatorname{Irr}_1$ is the set of characters of $F^\times$.

nodes.name: Standard additive character psi_F
nodes.statement: We let $\psi_F$ be the standard choice of additive character on $F$; namely if $F=\mathbb{R}$, then $\psi_{\mathbb{R}}(r)=e^{2\pi i r}$, and if $F=\mathbb C$, then $\psi_{\mathbb C}(z)=\psi_{\mathbb{R}}\circ\operatorname{Tr}_{\mathbb C/\mathbb{R}}(z)=e^{2\pi i(z+\bar{z})}$.
nodes.statement_short: $\psi_{\mathbb R}(r)=e^{2\pi i r}$ and $\psi_{\mathbb C}=\psi_{\mathbb R}\circ\operatorname{Tr}$.

nodes.name: Gamma function
nodes.statement: We let $\Gamma(s)$ be the gamma function.

nodes.name: Duplication formula
nodes.statement: Recall that $\Gamma(s)$ satisfies \[ \Gamma\left(\frac{s}{2}\right)\Gamma\left(\frac{s+1}{2}\right) =2^{1-s}\sqrt{\pi}\Gamma(s),\quad\text{(duplication formula)}. \]

nodes.name: Zeros and poles of the gamma function
nodes.statement: Also recall that $\Gamma(s)$ has no zeroes, and has infinitely many poles, which are precisely at $s=0, -1, -2, \dots$ and all of which are simple.
conclusions: has infinitely many poles, which are precisely at $s=0, -1, -2, \dots$ and all of which are simple

nodes.name: Weil group W_F
nodes.statement: We let $W_F$ be the Weil group of $F$.

nodes.name: Weil groups W_C and W_R
nodes.statement: So $W_{\mathbb C}=\mathbb C^\times$ and $W_{\mathbb{R}}=\mathbb C^\times\cup j\mathbb C^\times$ with $j^2=-1$ and $jzj^{-1}=\bar{z}$.

nodes.name: Abelianization of the Weil group
nodes.statement: Note that $F^\times\cong W_F^{ab}$.

nodes.name: Norm map W_R -> R^x
nodes.statement: W_{\mathbb{R}}\longrightarrow \mathbb{R}^\times, \quad z\mapsto z\bar{z},\; j\mapsto -1,
nodes.label: E:W_R

nodes.name: Characters chi_{-N,t} of C^x
nodes.statement: If $F=\mathbb C$, each character is of the form \[ \chi_{-N, t}(z):=z^{-N}\|z\|^t, \] where $N\in\mathbb{Z}$ and $t\in\mathbb C$.
nodes.statement_short: Every character of $\mathbb C^\times$ is $\chi_{-N,t}(z)=z^{-N}\|z\|^t$ with $N\in\mathbb Z$, $t\in\mathbb C$.

nodes.name: Complex conjugate of chi_{-N,t}
nodes.statement: Let us note that \[ \overline{\chi_{-N,t}}=\chi_{N, t-N}, \] where $\overline{\chi_{-N,t}}(z):=\overline{\chi_{-N,t}(z)}=\chi_{-N,t}(\bar{z})$ as usual.

nodes.name: Characters lambda_{epsilon,t} of R^x
nodes.statement: If $F=\mathbb{R}$, each character is of the form \[ \lambda_{\varepsilon, t}(r):=r^{-\varepsilon}|r|^t=\operatorname{sign}(r)^{\varepsilon}|r|^{t-\varepsilon},\quad r\in\mathbb{R}^\times, \] where $\varepsilon\in\{0,1\}$, $t\in\mathbb C$ and $\operatorname{sign}$ is the sign character.
nodes.statement_short: Every character of $\mathbb R^\times$ is $\lambda_{\varepsilon,t}(r)=r^{-\varepsilon}|r|^t$, $\varepsilon\in\{0,1\}$.

nodes.name: Irreducible representations of W_C
nodes.statement: If $F=\mathbb C$, an irreducible representation of $W_{\mathbb C}=\mathbb C^\times$ is 1-dimensional, namely a character on $\mathbb C^\times$, and hence of the form $\chi_{-N,t}$ as above.
conclusions: an irreducible representation of $W_{\mathbb C}=\mathbb C^\times$ is 1-dimensional

nodes.name: Parameter over C as sum of characters
nodes.statement: \varphi=\chi_{-N_1,t_1}\oplus\cdots\oplus\chi_{-N_n, t_n}.
nodes.label: E:general_parameter_C

nodes.name: Irreducible representations of W_R
nodes.statement: If $F=\mathbb{R}$, an irreducible representation of $W_{\mathbb{R}}$ is 1 or 2 dimensional. If it is 1-dimensional, it factors through $W_{\mathbb{R}}^{ab}\cong\mathbb{R}^\times$ and hence is identified with a character of the form $\lambda_{\varepsilon, t}$.
conclusions: an irreducible representation of $W_{\mathbb{R}}$ is 1 or 2 dimensional

nodes.name: Two-dimensional parameter phi_{-N,t}
nodes.statement: If it is 2-dimensional, it is of the form \[ \varphi_{-N,t}:=\operatorname{Ind}_{W_{\mathbb C}}^{W_{\mathbb{R}}}\chi_{-N,t}. \]
nodes.statement_short: $\varphi_{-N,t}$ is the induction of $\chi_{-N,t}$ from $W_{\mathbb C}$ to $W_{\mathbb R}$.

nodes.name: Computation of det(phi_{-N,t})
nodes.statement: From the definition of $W_{\mathbb{R}}$, we can see that $\det(\varphi_{-N,t})(z)=\chi_{-N, t}(z\bar{z})=\|z\|^{-N+2t}$ for $z\in\mathbb C^\times\subseteq W_{\mathbb{R}}$, and $\det(\varphi_{-N,t})(j)=-\chi_{-N,t}(-1)=-(-1)^N$.
nodes.statement_short: Evaluate the determinant of the induced representation on $z$ and on $j$.

nodes.name: Central character of phi_{-N,t}
nodes.statement: r\mapsto\operatorname{sign}(r) r^{-N}|r|^{2t}.
nodes.label: E:central_character

nodes.name: Decomposition of phi_{0,t}
nodes.statement: Let us mention that if $N=0$, the representation $\varphi_{-N,t}$ is not irreducible but we have \[ \varphi_{0, t}=\lambda_{0, t}\oplus\lambda_{1, t+1}. \]

nodes.name: Symmetry phi_{-N,t}=phi_{N,t-N}
nodes.statement: \varphi_{-N,t}=\varphi_{N, t-N}.
nodes.label: E:N>0

nodes.name: Irreducible 2-dimensional representations of W_R
nodes.statement: Hence we may assume $N>0$. Namely the irreducible 2-dimensional representations of $W_{\mathbb{R}}$ are precisely the representations of the form $\varphi_{-N,t}$ with $N>0$.
conclusions: the irreducible 2-dimensional representations of $W_{\mathbb{R}}$ are precisely the representations of the form $\varphi_{-N,t}$ with $N>0$

nodes.name: Parameter over R
nodes.statement: \varphi=\left(\lambda_{\varepsilon_1,t_1}\oplus\cdots\oplus\lambda_{\varepsilon_p,t_p}\right)\oplus \left(\varphi_{-N_1,u_1}\oplus\cdots\oplus\varphi_{-N_q, u_q}\right)
nodes.label: E:general_parameter_R

nodes.name: L-factor of chi_{-N,t}
nodes.statement: \notag L(\chi_{-N, t})&=2(2\pi)^{-(t-\frac{N}{2}+\frac{|N|}{2})}\Gamma(t-\frac{N}{2}+\frac{|N|}{2})\\ &=\begin{cases}2(2\pi)^{-t}\Gamma(t),\quad\text{if $N\geq 0$};\\ 2(2\pi)^{-(t-N)}\Gamma(t-N),\quad\text{if $N<0$}, \end{cases}
nodes.label: E:L-factor-C

nodes.name: Epsilon-factor of chi_{-N,t}
nodes.statement: \epsilon(\chi_{-N,t},\psi_{\mathbb C})&=i^{|N|}.
nodes.label: E:ep-factor-C

nodes.name: Local factors invariant under conjugation
nodes.statement: Let us note that \begin{equation*} L(\chi_{-N, t})=L(\overline{\chi_{-N, t}})\quad\text{and}\quad \epsilon(\chi_{-N,t},\psi_{\mathbb C})=\epsilon(\overline{\chi_{-N,t}},\psi_{\mathbb C}). \end{equation*}

nodes.name: Local factors of a parameter over C
nodes.statement: In general, if $\varphi:W_{\mathbb C}\rightarrow\operatorname{GL}_n(\mathbb C)$ is an $n$-dimensional representation as in \eqref{E:general_parameter_C}, we define the local factors multiplicatively as \begin{align*} L(\varphi)&=L(\chi_{-N_1,t_1})\cdots L(\chi_{-N_n, t_n}),\\ \epsilon(\varphi,\psi_{\mathbb C}) &=\epsilon(\chi_{-N_1,t_1}, \psi_{\mathbb C})\cdots\epsilon(\chi_{-N_n, t_n}, \psi_{\mathbb C}). \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Local factors of a sum of characters are defined as the products of the factors of the summands.

nodes.name: L-factor of lambda_{epsilon,t}
nodes.statement: L(\lambda_{\varepsilon,t})&=\pi^{-\frac{t}{2}}\Gamma\left(\frac{t}{2}\right),
nodes.label: E:L-factor-R1

nodes.name: Epsilon-factor of lambda_{epsilon,t}
nodes.statement: \epsilon(\lambda_{\varepsilon,t},\psi_{\mathbb{R}})&=(-i)^\varepsilon.
nodes.label: E:ep-factor-R1

nodes.name: L-factor of phi_{-N,t}
nodes.statement: L(\varphi_{-N,t})&=L(\chi_{-N,t}) =\begin{cases}2(2\pi)^{-t}\Gamma(t),\quad\text{if $N\geq 0$};\\ 2(2\pi)^{-(t-N)}\Gamma(t-N),\quad\text{if $N<0$}, \end{cases}
nodes.label: E:L-factor-R2

nodes.name: Epsilon-factor of phi_{-N,t}
nodes.statement: \epsilon(\varphi_{-N,t},\psi_{\mathbb{R}})&=-i\cdot\epsilon(\chi_{-N,t},\psi_{\mathbb C})=-i^{|N|+1}.
nodes.label: E:ep-factor-R2

nodes.name: Local factors of a parameter over R
nodes.statement: In general, if $\varphi:W_{\mathbb{R}}\rightarrow\operatorname{GL}_n(\mathbb C)$ is an $n$-dimensional representation as in \eqref{E:general_parameter_R}, we again define the local factors multiplicatively as \begin{align*} L(\varphi)&=L(\lambda_{\varepsilon_1,t_1})\cdots L(\lambda_{\varepsilon_p,t_p})\cdot L(\varphi_{-N_1,u_1})\cdots L(\chi_{-N_q, u_q})\\ \epsilon(\varphi,\psi_{\mathbb{R}}) &=\epsilon(\lambda_{\varepsilon_1,t_1}, \psi_{\mathbb{R}})\cdots\epsilon(\lambda_{\varepsilon_p,t_p}, \psi_{\mathbb{R}})\cdot \epsilon(\varphi_{-N_1,u_1}, \psi_{\mathbb{R}})\cdots \epsilon(\chi_{-N_q, u_q},\psi_{\mathbb{R}}). \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Local factors of a real parameter are the products of those of its 1- and 2-dimensional constituents.

nodes.name: L-factor of phi_{0,t} via duplication formula
nodes.statement: Let us note that for the parameter $\varphi_{0, t}$, we can check that $L(\varphi_{0, t})=L(\chi_{0, t})=2(2\pi)^{-t}\Gamma(t)$, which is indeed equal to $L(\lambda_{0,t})L(\lambda_{1,t+1})=\pi^{-t/2}\Gamma(\frac{t}{2})\cdot\pi^{-(t+1)/2}\Gamma(\frac{t+1}{2})$ by the duplication formula.
nodes.statement_short: $L(\varphi_{0,t})=L(\lambda_{0,t})L(\lambda_{1,t+1})$, by the duplication formula.
conclusions: $L(\varphi_{0, t})=L(\chi_{0, t})=2(2\pi)^{-t}\Gamma(t)$, which is indeed equal to $L(\lambda_{0,t})L(\lambda_{1,t+1})=\pi^{-t/2}\Gamma(\frac{t}{2})\cdot\pi^{-(t+1)/2}\Gamma(\frac{t+1}{2})$
also_stated_at: However, let us note that for the parameter $\varphi_{0, t}$, we can check that $L(\varphi_{0, t})=L(\chi_{0, t})=2(2\pi)^{-t}\Gamma(t)$, since it is indeed equal to $L(\lambda_{0,t})L(\lambda_{1,t+1})=\pi^{-t/2}\Gamma(\frac{t}{2})\cdot\pi^{-(t+1)/2}\Gamma(\frac{t+1}{2})$ by the duplication formula.

nodes.name: Twisted parameter over C
nodes.statement: \varphi\otimes\chi_{-M,s} =\chi_{-(N_1+M), t_1+s}\oplus\cdots\oplus\chi_{-(N_n+M), t_n+s}.
nodes.label: E:twisted_general_parameter_C

nodes.name: Twist of lambda_{epsilon,t} by lambda_{delta,s}
nodes.statement: Assume $F=\mathbb{R}$. Let $\lambda_{\delta, s}$ be a character on $\mathbb{R}^\times$. For the 1-dimensional parameter $\lambda_{\varepsilon,t}$, the twist by $\lambda_{\delta,s}$ is given by \[ \lambda_{\varepsilon, t}\otimes\lambda_{\delta,s}= \lambda_{\varepsilon+\delta\,(\operatorname{mod} 2),\, t+s-\gamma}, \;\text{ where }\; \gamma=\begin{cases}2\quad\text{if $\varepsilon=\delta=1$};\\ 0,\quad\text{otherwise}. \end{cases} \]
nodes.statement_short: $\lambda_{\varepsilon,t}\otimes\lambda_{\delta,s}=\lambda_{\varepsilon+\delta,t+s-\gamma}$ with $\gamma=2$ iff $\varepsilon=\delta=1$.

nodes.name: Twist of phi_{-N,t} by lambda_{delta,s}
nodes.statement: For the 2-dimensional parameter $\varphi_{-N,t}=\operatorname{Ind}_{W_{\mathbb C}}^{W_{\mathbb{R}}}\chi_{-N, t}$, the twisted parameter $\varphi_{-N,t}\otimes\lambda_{\delta,s}$ is computed as \begin{align*} \varphi_{-N,t}\otimes\lambda_{\delta,s} &=\operatorname{Ind}_{W_{\mathbb C}}^{W_{\mathbb{R}}}(\chi_{-N, t}\otimes(\lambda_{\delta, s}\circ N_{\mathbb C/\mathbb{R}}))\\ &=\operatorname{Ind}_{W_{\mathbb C}}^{W_{\mathbb{R}}}(\chi_{-N, t}\otimes\chi_{0, s-\delta})\\ &=\operatorname{Ind}_{W_{\mathbb C}}^{W_{\mathbb{R}}}\chi_{-N, t+s-\delta}, \end{align*} namely \[ \varphi_{-N, t}\otimes\lambda_{\delta, s}=\varphi_{-N, t+s-\delta}. \]
nodes.statement_short: $\varphi_{-N,t}\otimes\lambda_{\delta,s}=\varphi_{-N,t+s-\delta}$, computed by inducing the twisted character.

nodes.name: L-factor of GL(2)xGL(1) twist
nodes.statement: L(\varphi_{-N, t}\otimes\lambda_{\delta, s})&=\begin{cases} 2(2\pi)^{-(t+s-\delta)}\Gamma(t+s-\delta),\quad\text{if $N\geq 0$};\\ 2(2\pi)^{-(t+s-\delta-N)}\Gamma(t+s-\delta-N) \quad\text{if $N<0$}; \end{cases}
nodes.label: E:GL(2)xGL(1)_L

nodes.name: Epsilon-factor of GL(2)xGL(1) twist
nodes.statement: \epsilon(\varphi_{-N, t}\otimes\lambda_{\delta, s}, \psi_{\mathbb{R}})&=-i^{|N|+1}.
nodes.label: E:GL(2)xGL(2)_ep

nodes.name: GL(1)-twist of a parameter over R
nodes.statement: If $\varphi:W_{\mathbb{R}}\rightarrow\operatorname{GL}_n(\mathbb C)$ is an $n$-dimensional representation as in \eqref{E:general_parameter_R}, we have \[ \varphi\otimes\lambda_{\delta, s}= \left(\lambda_{\delta_1,t_1+s-\gamma_1} \oplus\cdots\oplus\lambda_{\delta_p,t_p+s-\gamma_p}\right)\oplus \left(\varphi_{-N_1,u_1+s-\delta}\oplus\cdots\oplus\varphi_{-N_q, u_q+s-\delta}\right), \] where $\delta_i=\varepsilon_i+\delta\pmod{2}$, and $\gamma_i=2$ if $\varepsilon_i=\delta=1$ and $\gamma_i=0$ otherwise.
nodes.statement_short: Twisting a real parameter by $\lambda_{\delta,s}$ twists each 1- and 2-dimensional constituent as above.

nodes.name: Tensor product of two 2-dimensional parameters
nodes.statement: Assume $F=\mathbb{R}$. Let $\varphi_{-N,t}$ and $\varphi_{-M,s}$ be 2-dimensional representations of $W_{\mathbb{R}}$ as above with $N, M > 0$. Then one can see \begin{align*} \varphi_{-N,t}\otimes\varphi_{-M,s}=& \left(\operatorname{Ind}_{W_{\mathbb C}}^{W_{\mathbb{R}}}\chi_{-N,t}\right)\otimes \left(\operatorname{Ind}_{W_{\mathbb C}}^{W_{\mathbb{R}}}\chi_{-M,s}\right)\\ =&\left(\operatorname{Ind}_{W_{\mathbb C}}^{W_{\mathbb{R}}}\chi_{-N,t}\cdot\chi_{-M,s}\right)\oplus \left(\operatorname{Ind}_{W_{\mathbb C}}^{W_{\mathbb{R}}}\chi_{-N,t}\cdot\overline{\chi_{-M,s}}\right)\\ =&\left(\operatorname{Ind}_{W_{\mathbb C}}^{W_{\mathbb{R}}}\chi_{-(N+M),t+s}\right)\oplus \left(\operatorname{Ind}_{W_{\mathbb C}}^{W_{\mathbb{R}}}\chi_{-N,t}\cdot\chi_{M,s-M}\right)\\ =&\varphi_{-(N+M), t+s}\oplus \left(\operatorname{Ind}_{W_{\mathbb C}}^{W_{\mathbb{R}}}\chi_{-(N-M),t+s-M}\right)\\ =&\varphi_{-(N+M), t+s}\oplus\varphi_{-(N-M), t+s-M}. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: $\varphi_{-N,t}\otimes\varphi_{-M,s}=\varphi_{-(N+M),t+s}\oplus\varphi_{-(N-M),t+s-M}$ by Mackey theory.
assumptions: $\varphi_{-N,t}$ and $\varphi_{-M,s}$ be 2-dimensional representations of $W_{\mathbb{R}}$ as above with $N, M > 0$

nodes.name: L-factor of GL(2)xGL(2) twist
nodes.statement: L(\varphi_{-N,t}\otimes\varphi_{-M,s})&=4(2\pi)^{-2(t+s)+\min\{N, M\}}\cdot\Gamma(t+s)\cdot \Gamma(t+s-\min\{N, M\})
nodes.label: E:GL(2)xGL(2)_L

nodes.name: Epsilon-factor of GL(2)xGL(2) twist
nodes.statement: \epsilon(\varphi_{-N,t}\otimes\varphi_{-M,s})&=(-1)^{\max\{N, M\}}.
nodes.label: E:GL(2)xGL(2)_ep

nodes.name: Archimedean local Langlands correspondence
nodes.statement: By the archimedean local Langlands correspondence, originally established by Langlands (\cite{Langlands}), there is a one-to-one correspondence between the set $\operatorname{Irr}_n$ and the set $\Phi_n$ of all continuous $n$-dimensional representations of $W_F$.
conclusions: there is a one-to-one correspondence between the set $\operatorname{Irr}_n$ and the set $\Phi_n$ of all continuous $n$-dimensional representations of $W_F$

nodes.name: Local factors of pairs (Artin type)
nodes.statement: If $\pi_1\in\operatorname{Irr}_n$ and $\pi_2\in\operatorname{Irr}_t$ correspond to $\varphi_1\in\Phi_n$ and $\varphi_2\in\Phi_t$, respectively, then the local factors are defined to be \begin{align*} L(s,\pi_1\times\pi_2)&=L(\varphi_1\otimes\varphi_2|\cdot|_F^s)\\ \epsilon(s,\pi_1\times\pi_2,\psi_F)&= \epsilon(\varphi_1\otimes\varphi_2|\cdot|_F^s,\psi_F), \end{align*} where $|\cdot|_{\mathbb C}=\|\cdot\|$ and $|\cdot|_{\mathbb{R}}=|\cdot|$.
nodes.statement_short: Rankin-Selberg factors of $\pi_1\times\pi_2$ are the Artin factors of $\varphi_1\otimes\varphi_2|\cdot|^s$.

nodes.name: Central character under local Langlands
nodes.statement: Further if $\varphi\in\operatorname{Irr}_n$ corresponds to $\varphi_\pi\in\Phi_n$ and if $\omega_\pi$ is the central character of $\pi$, we have \[ \omega_\pi=\det(\varphi_\pi). \]

nodes.name: Central character of GL_2(R) representation
nodes.statement: In particular, if $\pi$ is a representation of $\operatorname{GL}_2(\mathbb{R})$ such that $\varphi_\pi=\varphi_{-N,t}$, then $\omega_\pi$ is as in \eqref{E:central_character}.
assumptions: $\pi$ is a representation of $\operatorname{GL}_2(\mathbb{R})$ such that $\varphi_\pi=\varphi_{-N,t}$

nodes.name: Partial order on C
nodes.statement: We define a partial order $\preceq$ on the set $\mathbb C$ of complex numbers as follows: For $t_1,t_2\in\mathbb C$, \[ t_1\preceq t_2\quad\text{if}\quad t_2-t_1\in\mathbb{Z}^{\geq 0}, \] and otherwise we say they are \emph{incomparable}.
nodes.statement_short: $t_1\preceq t_2$ iff $t_2-t_1$ is a nonnegative integer; otherwise incomparable.

nodes.name: Strict order prec
nodes.statement: We use the symbol $\prec$ for strict inequality, namely \[ t_1\prec t_2\quad\text{if}\quad t_1\preceq t_2\text{ but } t_1\neq t_2. \]

nodes.name: Partial order versus poles of Gamma
nodes.statement: Then one can check that $t_1\prec t_2$ if and only if \begin{equation*} \{\text{poles of $\Gamma(s+t_1)$}\}\supsetneq \{\text{poles of $\Gamma(s+t_2)$}\}, \end{equation*} and $t_1$ and $t_2$ are incomparable if and only if \begin{equation*} \{\text{poles of $\Gamma(s+t_1)$}\}\cap \{\text{poles of $\Gamma(s+t_2)$}\}=\emptyset. \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: $t_1\prec t_2$ iff the poles of $\Gamma(s+t_1)$ strictly contain those of $\Gamma(s+t_2)$; incomparable iff disjoint.
conclusions: $t_1\prec t_2$ if and only if \begin{equation*} \{\text{poles of $\Gamma(s+t_1)$}\}\supsetneq \{\text{poles of $\Gamma(s+t_2)$}\}, \end{equation*}
$t_1$ and $t_2$ are incomparable if and only if \begin{equation*} \{\text{poles of $\Gamma(s+t_1)$}\}\cap \{\text{poles of $\Gamma(s+t_2)$}\}=\emptyset. \end{equation*}

nodes.name: Minimal element
nodes.statement: If $A$ is a finite set of complex numbers and $t\in A$ is a minimal element in $A$ (\text{i.e.\ } whenever $t'\in A$ is such that $t'\preceq t$, we have $t'=t$), we say $t$ is {\it minimal in} $A$.
differentia: whenever $t'\in A$ is such that $t'\preceq t$, we have $t'=t$

nodes.name: Maximal pole
nodes.statement: Let $F(s)$ be a function on $\mathbb C$. If $F(s)$ has a pole at $s=t$ and if it is maximal among the poles of $F(s)$ with respect to $\preceq$ (\text{i.e.\ } if $F(s)$ has a pole at $s=t'$ and $t\preceq t'$, then $t=t'$), then we call the pole at $s=t$ a {\it maximal pole} of $F(s)$.
differentia: it is maximal among the poles of $F(s)$ with respect to $\preceq$

nodes.name: Maximal pole of Gamma(s+t)
nodes.statement: In particular, for a fixed $t\in\mathbb C$, the gamma function $\Gamma(s+t)$ has a unique maximal pole at $s=-t$.
conclusions: the gamma function $\Gamma(s+t)$ has a unique maximal pole at $s=-t$

nodes.name: Maximal poles of a product of gamma functions
nodes.statement: More generally, a product $\prod_{i=1}^n\Gamma(s+t_i)$ of gamma functions has a maximal pole precisely at $s=-t_i$ where $t_i$ is a minimal element in the set $\{t_1,\dots,t_n\}$.
conclusions: a product $\prod_{i=1}^n\Gamma(s+t_i)$ of gamma functions has a maximal pole precisely at $s=-t_i$ where $t_i$ is a minimal element in the set $\{t_1,\dots,t_n\}$

nodes.name: Gamma-product identity
nodes.statement: F(s)\cdot\prod_{i=1}^m\Gamma(s+t_i)=\prod_{j=1}^{m'}\Gamma(s+t'_j)
nodes.label: E:Lemma

nodes.name: Proof of the Gamma-product lemma
nodes.statement: This is almost immediate if one looks at the maximal poles of both sides. Namely, if $t_k$ is minimal in $\{t_1,\cdots,t_m\}$, the left hand side has a maximal pole at $s=-t_k$, and hence the right hand side has a maximal pole at $s=-t_k$. But each maximal pole of the right hand side occurs at $s=-t'_l$ for some $t'_l$ which is minimal in $\{t'_1,\dots,t'_{m'}\}$. Hence $t_k=t'_l$ for some $l$. After reordering the indices, if necessary, we may assume $t_1=t'_1$. Hence \eqref{E:Lemma} is written as \[ F(s)\cdot\prod_{i=2}^m\Gamma(s+t_i)=\prod_{j=2}^{m'}\Gamma(s+t'_j). \] By arguing inductively, one proves the lemma.
nodes.statement_short: Induction on the number of factors: match a maximal pole on both sides, cancel the corresponding gamma factors.

nodes.name: Match a maximal pole
nodes.statement: This is almost immediate if one looks at the maximal poles of both sides. Namely, if $t_k$ is minimal in $\{t_1,\cdots,t_m\}$, the left hand side has a maximal pole at $s=-t_k$, and hence the right hand side has a maximal pole at $s=-t_k$.
nodes.statement_short: A minimal $t_k$ gives a maximal pole at $s=-t_k$ on both sides.

nodes.name: Identify t_k with some t'_l
nodes.statement: But each maximal pole of the right hand side occurs at $s=-t'_l$ for some $t'_l$ which is minimal in $\{t'_1,\dots,t'_{m'}\}$. Hence $t_k=t'_l$ for some $l$.
nodes.statement_short: Maximal poles on the right come from minimal $t'_l$, so $t_k=t'_l$.

nodes.name: Cancel the matched factor
nodes.statement: After reordering the indices, if necessary, we may assume $t_1=t'_1$. Hence \eqref{E:Lemma} is written as \[ F(s)\cdot\prod_{i=2}^m\Gamma(s+t_i)=\prod_{j=2}^{m'}\Gamma(s+t'_j). \]
nodes.statement_short: Reorder so $t_1=t'_1$ and cancel one gamma factor from each side.

nodes.name: Conclude by induction
nodes.statement: By arguing inductively, one proves the lemma.
nodes.statement_short: Induct on the number of factors.

nodes.name: Introduce the parameters
nodes.statement: We will prove our main theorem for $F=\mathbb C$. Let $\pi$ and $\pi'$ be infinitesimal equivalence classes of irreducible admissible representations of $\operatorname{GL}_n(\mathbb C)$, and assume that their corresponding Langlands parameters $\varphi$ and $\varphi'$ are given by \begin{align*} \varphi&=\chi_{-N_1,t_1}\oplus\cdots\oplus\chi_{-N_n, t_n}\\ \varphi'&=\chi_{-N'_1,t'_1}\oplus\cdots\oplus\chi_{-N'_n, t'_n}. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Write the parameters of $\pi,\pi'$ as sums of characters.

nodes.name: L-equality for GL(1)-twists over C
nodes.statement: L(\varphi\otimes\chi_{-M, s})=L(\varphi'\otimes\chi_{-M, s})
nodes.label: E:L-equality-C0

nodes.name: Product L-equality over C
nodes.statement: \prod_{i=1}^nL(\chi_{-(N_i+M),t_i+s}) =\prod_{j=1}^nL(\chi_{-(N'_j+M),t'_j+s})
nodes.label: E:L-equality-C

nodes.name: Common constituent goal
nodes.statement: \chi_{-N_i, t_i}=\chi_{-N'_j, t'_j}
nodes.label: E:goal

nodes.name: Outline of three steps
nodes.statement: The basic idea of our proof is that we will examine ``maximal poles'' of both sides of \eqref{E:L-equality-C} for different choices of $M$. Our proof has three major steps, which is outlined as follows. In Step 1, we will show that $\{t_1,\dots, t_n\}=\{t'_1,\dots, t'_n\}$ as multisets. In Step 2, we will show that $\min\{N_1,\dots,N_n\}=\min\{N'_1,\dots,N'_n\}$. Finally in Step 3, we will finish up the proof of the theorem. In each of the steps we will choose an appropriate $M$.
nodes.statement_short: Outline: multisets of $t$'s, then minima of $N$'s, then conclusion.

nodes.name: Step 1: equal t-multisets
nodes.statement: \subsection{Step 1} Let us choose $M$ large enough so that $N_i+M> 0$ and $N'_j+M>0$ for all $i, j\in\{1,\cdots,n\}$. By \eqref{E:L-factor-C}, we can write \eqref{E:L-equality-C} as \[ F(s)\prod_{i=1}^n\Gamma(s+t_i)=\prod_{j=1}^n\Gamma(s+t'_j) \] for some function $F(s)$ without a pole or zero. Hence by Lemma \ref{L:Lemma}, we have \[ \{t_1,\dots, t_n\}=\{t'_1,\dots, t'_n\} \] as multisets.
nodes.statement_short: Large $M$ makes all factors plain gamma functions; Lemma 3.1 gives $\{t_i\}=\{t'_j\}$.

nodes.name: Choose M large
nodes.statement: Let us choose $M$ large enough so that $N_i+M> 0$ and $N'_j+M>0$ for all $i, j\in\{1,\cdots,n\}$. By \eqref{E:L-factor-C}, we can write \eqref{E:L-equality-C} as \[ F(s)\prod_{i=1}^n\Gamma(s+t_i)=\prod_{j=1}^n\Gamma(s+t'_j) \] for some function $F(s)$ without a pole or zero.
nodes.statement_short: Choose $M$ large and rewrite (4.2) as a gamma-product identity.

nodes.name: Apply the lemma
nodes.statement: Hence by Lemma \ref{L:Lemma}, we have \[ \{t_1,\dots, t_n\}=\{t'_1,\dots, t'_n\} \] as multisets.
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 3.1 gives equal multisets of $t$'s.

nodes.name: Gamma identity with epsilon_j
nodes.statement: F(s)\prod_{i=1}^n\Gamma(s+t_i)=\prod_{j=1}^n\Gamma(s+t'_j+\varepsilon_j),
nodes.label: E:L-equality-C1

nodes.name: Locate a maximal pole
nodes.statement: Now the left hand side of \eqref{E:L-equality-C1} has a maximal pole at $s=-t_k$ for some $t_k$ which is minimal in $\{t_1,\dots,t_n\}$. Then $t_k=t'_l+\varepsilon_l$ for some $l$ and $t'_l+\varepsilon_l$ is minimal in $\{t'_1+\varepsilon_1,\dots,t'_n+\varepsilon_n\}$.
nodes.statement_short: A maximal pole on the left matches a minimal $t'_l+\varepsilon_l$.

nodes.name: Exclude epsilon_l = 1
nodes.statement: Assume $\varepsilon_l=1$. Then we have $t'_l+\varepsilon_l=t_l+1$ by \eqref{E:relation2}, which implies $t_l+1=t_k$. But then $t_l\prec t_k$, which contradicts the minimality of $t_k$. Hence $\varepsilon_l=0$, namely $t_k=t'_l$.
nodes.statement_short: $\varepsilon_l=1$ contradicts minimality of $t_k$, so $t_k=t'_l$.

nodes.name: Gamma identity after cancelling
nodes.statement: F(s)\prod_{i\neq k}\Gamma(s+t_i)=\prod_{j\neq l}\Gamma(s+t'_j+\varepsilon_j).
nodes.label: E:L-equality-C2

nodes.name: Conclude N_min = N'_min
nodes.statement: By arguing inductively, one can show that $\varepsilon_j=0$ for all $j\in\{1,\dots,n\}$ which is a contradiction. Hence we must have $N'_{\min}\geq N_{\min}$. By symmetry, we can show that $N'_{\min}\leq N_{\min}$. Hence $N_{\min}=N'_{\min}$.
nodes.statement_short: Induction forces all $\varepsilon_j=0$, a contradiction; symmetry gives equality.

nodes.name: Ordering of N_i
nodes.statement: N_1=N_2=\cdots=N_d<N_{d+1}\leq\cdots\leq N_n,
nodes.label: E:relation1

nodes.name: Gamma identity for M=-N_1-1
nodes.statement: F(s)\prod_{i=1}^d\Gamma(s+t_i+1)\cdot\prod_{i=d+1}^n\Gamma(s+t_i) =\prod_{j=1}^n\Gamma(s+t'_j+\varepsilon_j)
nodes.label: E:L-equality-C3

nodes.name: Multisets A and B
nodes.statement: Let \begin{align*} A&:=A_1\cup A_2, \quad A_1:=\{t_i+1:i\in\{1,\dots,d\}\},\quad A_2:=\{t_i:i\in\{d+1,\dots,n\}\}\\ B&:=\{t'_j+\varepsilon_j: j\in\{1,\dots,n\}\}. \end{align*} Of course by Lemma \ref{L:Lemma}, we know $A=B$ as multisets.
nodes.statement_short: Define $A=A_1\cup A_2$ and $B$; Lemma 3.1 gives $A=B$.

nodes.name: Split into two cases
nodes.statement: We will again look at ``maximal poles'' of \eqref{E:L-equality-C3}, which correspond to minimal elements of $A=B$. We consider the following two cases, depending on whether a minimal element is in $A_1$ or $A_2$.
nodes.statement_short: Cases by whether a minimal element of $A$ lies in $A_1$ or $A_2$.

nodes.name: Case: minimal element in A_1
nodes.statement: First assume $t_k+1\in A_1$ with $k\leq d$ is minmal in $A$. By $A=B$, we have $t_k+1=t'_l+\varepsilon_l$ for some $l$, which is minimal in $B$. Assume $\varepsilon_l=1$. Then this means $N'_l=N_1=N_k$ and $t_k=t'_l$. Hence we have \eqref{E:goal} with $i=k$ and $j=l$. Assume $\varepsilon_l=0$. First assume $\varepsilon_k=0$. Then $t'_k+\varepsilon_k=t_k=t'_l+\varepsilon_l-1$, namely $t'_k+\varepsilon_k\prec t'_l+\varepsilon_l$, which contradicts the minimality of $t'_l+\varepsilon_l$. Hence $\varepsilon_k=1$, which implies $N'_k=N_1=N_k$. Since $t_k=t'_k$ by \eqref{E:relation2}, the equality \eqref{E:goal} is satisfied with $i=j=k$.
nodes.statement_short: A minimal $t_k+1\in A_1$ yields (4.3) in each subcase.

nodes.name: Case: minimal element in A_2
nodes.statement: Next assume that $t_k\in A_2$ with $k>d$ is minmal in $A$. By $A=B$, we know that $t_k=t'_l+\varepsilon_l$ for some $l$, which is minimal in $B$. Assume $\varepsilon_l=1$, so $t_k=t'_l+1=t_l+1$. Then $t_l\prec t_k$. Since $t_k$ is minimal in $A$, we must have $l\leq d$. Hence $N_l=N_1$. Also since $\varepsilon_l=1$ implies $N'_l=N_1$, we have $N'_l=N_l$. Hence, we have \eqref{E:goal} with $i=j=l$. Finally assume $\varepsilon_l=0$, \text{i.e.\ } $t_k=t'_l$. Then we can reorder the indices $j$ for the multiset $B$ by swapping $k$ and $l$ without changing the relations \eqref{E:relation2} and \eqref{E:relation1}. So we can cancel $\Gamma(s+t_k)$ from both sides of \eqref{E:L-equality-C3}. We can now argue inductively by repeating the above arguments until we obtain \eqref{E:goal}. The proof is complete.
nodes.statement_short: A minimal $t_k\in A_2$ gives (4.3) or allows cancelling and repeating.

nodes.name: L-equality for GL(1)-twists over R
nodes.statement: L(\varphi\otimes\lambda_{\varepsilon,s})=L(\varphi'\otimes\lambda_{\varepsilon,s})
nodes.label: E:character-twist

nodes.name: L-equality for GL(2)-twists over R
nodes.statement: L(\varphi\otimes\varphi_{-M,s})=L(\varphi'\otimes\varphi_{-M,s})
nodes.label: E:GL(2)-twist

nodes.name: Write the parameters
nodes.statement: Let us write \begin{align*} \varphi&=\left(\lambda_{\varepsilon_1,t_1}\oplus\cdots\oplus\lambda_{\varepsilon_p,t_p}\right)\oplus \left(\varphi_{-N_1,u_1}\oplus\cdots\oplus\varphi_{-N_q, u_q}\right)\\ \varphi'&=\left(\lambda_{\varepsilon'_1,t'_1}\oplus\cdots\oplus\lambda_{\varepsilon'_{p'},t'_{p'}}\right)\oplus \left(\varphi_{-N'_1,u'_1}\oplus\cdots\oplus\varphi_{-N'_{q'} u'_{q'}}\right) \end{align*} where we may assume $N_i>0$ and $N'_j>0$ for all $i, j$. Note that the numbers of 1-dimensional constituents for $\varphi$ and $\varphi'$ are, respectively, $p$ and $p'$, and those for 2-dimensional ones are, respectively, $q$ and $q'$, so $n=p+2q=p'+2q'$.
nodes.statement_short: Decompose $\varphi,\varphi'$ into 1- and 2-dimensional constituents.

nodes.name: Outline
nodes.statement: The proof has three steps, and the basic philosophy is the same as the complex case in that we choose appropriate twists and examine ``maximal poles''. In Step 1, we will show $\{u_1, ..., u_q\}=\{u'_1, ..., u'_{q'} \}$ and $\{t_1-\varepsilon_1, ..., t_p-\varepsilon_p\}=\{t'_1-\varepsilon'_1, ..., t'_{p'}-\varepsilon'_{p'}\}$ as multisets, which also implies $p=p'$ and $q=q'$. In Step 2, we will show the 1-dimensional constituents are equal. Finally in Step 3, we will show the 2-dimensional constituents are equal.
nodes.statement_short: Outline of the three steps.

nodes.name: GL(2)-twist L-factors
nodes.statement: Consider the twist by $\varphi_{-M, s}$ with $M\geq 0$. Since all the $N_i$'s and $N'_j$'s are positive, \eqref{E:GL(2)xGL(1)_L} and \eqref{E:GL(2)xGL(2)_L} give \begin{align*} L(\varphi\otimes\varphi_{-M, s})&=F(s) \prod_{i=1}^{p}\Gamma(s+t_i-\varepsilon_i)\cdot \prod_{i=1}^{q}\Gamma(s+u_i)\cdot\Gamma(s+u_i-\min\{M, N_i\})\\ L(\varphi'\otimes\varphi_{-M, s})&=F'(s) \prod_{j=1}^{p'}\Gamma(s+t'_j-\varepsilon'_j)\cdot \prod_{j=1}^{q'}\Gamma(s+u'_j)\cdot\Gamma(s+u'_j-\min\{M, N'_j\}), \end{align*} where $F(s)$ and $F'(s)$ are functions without a zero or pole. And the equality \eqref{E:GL(2)-twist} implies those two are equal.
nodes.statement_short: Compute $L(\varphi\otimes\varphi_{-M,s})$ as gamma products.

nodes.name: Multiset identity M=0
nodes.statement: &\{t_1-\varepsilon_1,\dots,t_p-\varepsilon_p\}\cup\{u_1,\dots,u_q\}\cup\{u_1,\dots,u_q\}\\ \notag=&\{t'_1-\varepsilon'_1,\dots,t'_{p'}-\varepsilon'_{p'}\}\cup\{u'_1,\dots,u'_{q'}\}\cup\{u'_1,\dots,u'_{q'}\},
nodes.label: E:multisets_t_u-0

nodes.name: Multiset identity M=1
nodes.statement: &\{t_1-\varepsilon_1,\dots,t_p-\varepsilon_p\}\cup\{u_1,\dots,u_q\}\cup\{u_1-1,\dots,u_q-1\}\\ \notag=&\{t'_1-\varepsilon'_1,\dots,t'_{p'}-\varepsilon'_{p'}\}\cup\{u'_1,\dots,u'_{q'}\} \cup\{u'_1-1,\dots,u'_{q'}-1\}
nodes.label: E:multisets_t_u-1

nodes.name: Equal multisets t-epsilon
nodes.statement: \{t_1-\varepsilon_1,\dots,t_p-\varepsilon_p\}&=\{t'_1-\varepsilon'_1,\dots,t'_{p'}-\varepsilon'_{p'}\}
nodes.label: E:multisets_t-ep

nodes.name: Case: minimal t_k - epsilon_k
nodes.statement:
First assume $t_k-\varepsilon_k$ is minimal in the left hand side of \eqref{E:multisets_t_u-0}. Then either $t_k-\varepsilon_k=t'_l-\varepsilon'_{l'}$ for some $l$, or $t_k-\varepsilon_k=u'_l$. If the former is the case, 	ext{i.e.\ } \[ t_k-\varepsilon_k=t'_l-\varepsilon'_l, \] we can eliminate $t_k-\varepsilon_k$ from the left hand sides of both \eqref{E:multisets_t_u-0} and \eqref{E:multisets_t_u-1} and eliminate $t'_l-\varepsilon'_l$ from the right hand sides of both \eqref{E:multisets_t_u-0} and \eqref{E:multisets_t_u-1}, which allows us to shrink the multisets in those two equalities and obtain  egin{align*} &\{t_i-\varepsilon_i: i
eq k\}\cup\{u_1,\dots,u_q\}\cup\{u_1,\dots,u_q\}\ 
otag=&\{t'_j-\varepsilon'_j: j
eq l\}\cup\{u'_1,\dots,u'_{q'}\}\cup\{u'_1,\dots,u'_{q'}\}, \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Minimal $t_k-\varepsilon_k$ matches either some $t'_l-\varepsilon'_l$ or some $u'_l$; in both cases shrink.

nodes.name: Case: minimal u_k
nodes.statement: Next assume $u_k$ is a minimal element in the left hand side of \eqref{E:multisets_t_u-0}. Then either $u_k=u'_l$ or $u_k=t'_l-\varepsilon_l'$ for some $l$. If the former is the case, one can shrink both sides of \eqref{E:multisets_t_u-0} and \eqref{E:multisets_t_u-1} as above. If the latter is the case, by arguing in the same way one can obtain $u_k-1=u'_m-1$ for some $m$, which gives $u_k=u'_m$ and allows us to shrink the multisets in \eqref{E:multisets_t_u-0} and \eqref{E:multisets_t_u-1} as before.
nodes.statement_short: Minimal $u_k$ is handled the same way.

nodes.name: Summarize induction
nodes.statement: To summarize, at each step one can obtain either $t_i-\varepsilon_i=t'_j-\varepsilon'_j$ or $u_i=u'_j$ for some $i, j$, and by eliminating this element from \eqref{E:multisets_t_u-0} and \eqref{E:multisets_t_u-1}, one can shrink the multisets from those two equalities. But the resulting equalities are of the same form, and hence we can apply the same argument to those two shrunken equalities. By repeating the process, one can obtain \eqref{E:multisets_t-ep} and \eqref{E:multisets_u}, which also imply $p=p'$ and $q=q'$.
nodes.statement_short: Repeating the elimination gives (5.5) and (5.6).

nodes.name: Twist by lambda_{0,s}
nodes.statement: We will show the 1-dimensional constituents of $\varphi$ and $\varphi'$ are equal. By twisting by $\lambda_{0,s}$, we have \begin{align*} \varphi\otimes\lambda_{0, s} &=\left(\lambda_{\varepsilon_1, t_1+s}\oplus\cdots\oplus\lambda_{\varepsilon_p, t_p+s}\right) \oplus\left(\varphi_{-N_1, u_1+s}\oplus\cdots\oplus \varphi_{-N_q, u_q+s}\right)\\ \varphi'\otimes\lambda_{0, s} &=\left(\lambda_{\varepsilon'_1, t'_1+s}\oplus\cdots\oplus\lambda_{\varepsilon'_p, t'_p+s}\right) \oplus\left(\varphi_{-N'_1, u'_1+s}\oplus\cdots\oplus \varphi_{-N'_q, u'_q+s}\right), \end{align*} so the equality $L(\varphi\otimes\lambda_{0,s})=L(\varphi'\otimes\lambda_{0,s})$ implies \[ F(s)\prod_{i=1}^{p}\Gamma\left(\frac{s+t_i}{2}\right)\cdot\prod_{i=1}^q\Gamma(s+u_i) =\prod_{j=1}^{p}\Gamma\left(\frac{s+t'_j}{2}\right)\cdot\prod_{j=1}^q\Gamma(s+u'_j), \] where $F(s)$ is a function without a zero or pole.
nodes.statement_short: Twisting by $\lambda_{0,s}$ gives a gamma-product identity.

nodes.name: Reduce to one constituent
nodes.statement: By using \eqref{E:multisets_t-ep} and \eqref{E:multisets_t}, we will show that the 1-dimensional constituents of $\varphi$ and $\varphi'$ are equal. But of course, by induction, it suffices to show $\lambda_{\varepsilon_i,t_i}=\lambda_{\varepsilon'_j,t'_j}$ for some $i$ and $j$. We will show this by examining minimal elements in those multisets.
nodes.statement_short: By induction it suffices to match one 1-dimensional constituent.

nodes.name: Minimal t_k, equal signs
nodes.statement: First, let us note that since we have \eqref{E:multisets_t}, we may reorder the indices so that $t_i=t'_i$ for all $i\in\{1,\dots,n\}$. Let $t_k=t'_k$ be minimal in $\{t_1,\dots,t_p\}$. Clearly if $\varepsilon_k=\varepsilon'_k$, then $\lambda_{\varepsilon_k, t_k}=\lambda_{\varepsilon'_k, t'_k}$, so we are done.
nodes.statement_short: Align $t_i=t'_i$; if $\varepsilon_k=\varepsilon'_k$ we are done.

nodes.name: Different signs
nodes.statement: So let us assume $\varepsilon_k\neq\varepsilon'_k$. By symmetry, we may assume $\varepsilon_k=1$ and $\varepsilon'_k=0$. Note, then, that $t_k-\varepsilon_k$ is minimal in $\{t_1-\varepsilon_1,\dots,t_p-\varepsilon_p\}$. By \eqref{E:multisets_t-ep}, we must have $t_k-\varepsilon_k=t'_l-\varepsilon'_l$ for some $l$. Assume $\varepsilon'_l= 0$. Then $t_k-1=t'_l$, which implies $t'_l=t_l\prec t_k$. This contradicts the minimality of $t_k$. Hence $\varepsilon'_l=1=\varepsilon_k$. Then $t_k-\varepsilon_k=t'_l-\varepsilon'_l$ implies $t_l=t'_k$. Namely we have $\lambda_{\varepsilon_k,t_k}=\lambda_{\varepsilon'_l, t'_l}$. This completes the proof that $\varphi$ and $\varphi'$ have the same 1-dimensional constituents.
nodes.statement_short: If $\varepsilon_k\ne\varepsilon'_k$, minimality and (5.5) give a matching constituent.

nodes.name: Reduce to 2-dimensional part
nodes.statement: Finally, we will show that the 2-dimensional constituents are equal. Since we have already shown the 1-dimensional constituents are equal, we may assume \begin{align*} \varphi&=\varphi_{-N_1,u_1}\oplus\cdots\oplus\varphi_{-N_q, u_q}\\ \varphi'&=\varphi_{-N'_1,u'_1}\oplus\cdots\oplus\varphi_{-N'_{q'} u'_{q}}. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Remove the equal 1-dimensional constituents.

nodes.name: Gamma identity with M'_j
nodes.statement: F(s)\prod_{i=1}^q\Gamma(s+u_i-N_{\min})=\prod_{j=1}^q\Gamma(s+u'_j-M'_j), \quad M'_j=\min\{N'_j, N_{\min}\},
nodes.label: E:M=M'_j

nodes.name: Gamma identity over J
nodes.statement: F(s)\prod_{i\in J}\Gamma(s+u_i-N_{\min})=\prod_{j\in J}\Gamma(s+u'_j-N'_j).
nodes.label: E:M=M'_j2

nodes.name: Contradiction and N_min equality
nodes.statement: By Lemma \ref{L:Lemma}, we have \[ \{u_i-N_{\min}: i\in J\}=\{u'_j-N'_j: j\in J\} \] as multisets. Now suppose $u_k-N_{\min}$ is minimal in the left hand side, which is the same as supposing $u_k$ is minimal in $\{u_i: i\in J\}$. There exists $l\in J$ such that $u_k-N_{\min}=u'_l-N'_l$, which gives $u_k=u'_l+(N_{\min}-N'_l)$. Since $N_{\min}-N'_l>0$, this implies $u_l=u'_l\prec u_k$, which contradicts the minimality of $u_k$. Hence $N'_{\min}\geq N_{\min}$. By symmetry, we have $N'_{\min}\leq N_{\min}$, namely $N'_{\min}=N_{\min}$.
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 3.1 and minimality give a contradiction, so $N_{\min}=N'_{\min}$.

nodes.name: Ordering of N_i (real)
nodes.statement: 0<N_1=\cdots=N_{d}<N_{d+1}\leq\cdots\leq N_q.
nodes.label: E:relation1-R

nodes.name: Gamma identity for M=N_1+1
nodes.statement: F(s)\prod_{i=1}^d\Gamma(s+u_i-N_1)\prod_{i=d+1}^q\Gamma(s+u_i-N_1-1) =\prod_{j=1}^q\Gamma(s+u_i-N_1-1+\varepsilon_j),
nodes.label: E:L-equality-R3

nodes.name: Shifted gamma identity
nodes.statement: F(s+N_1+1)\prod_{i=1}^d\Gamma(s+u_i+1)\cdot\prod_{i=d+1}^q\Gamma(s+u_i) =\prod_{j=1}^q\Gamma(s+u_i+\varepsilon_j).
nodes.label: E:L-equality-R3-1

nodes.name: Local converse theorem for GL_2(R), GL_3(R) with central character
nodes.statement: Let $n=2$ or $3$. Assume $\pi, \pi'\in\operatorname{Irr}_n$ are such that \[ L(s, \pi\times\lambda)=L(s, \pi'\times\lambda) \] for all characters $\lambda$ on $\mathbb{R}^\times$. Further assume that the central characters of $\pi$ and $\pi'$ are equal. Then $\pi=\pi'$.
nodes.statement_short: For $n=2,3$, $\operatorname{GL}(1)$-twisted $L$-factors plus the central character determine $\pi\in\operatorname{Irr}_n$ over $\mathbb R$.
assumptions: $\pi, \pi'\in\operatorname{Irr}_n$ are such that \[ L(s, \pi\times\lambda)=L(s, \pi'\times\lambda) \] for all characters $\lambda$ on $\mathbb{R}^\times$
the central characters of $\pi$ and $\pi'$ are equal

nodes.name: Parameter phi as sum of three characters
nodes.statement: \varphi&=\lambda_{\varepsilon_1, t_1}\oplus\lambda_{\varepsilon_2, t_2}\oplus\lambda_{\varepsilon_3, t_3}
nodes.label: E:1+1+1

nodes.name: Parameter phi' of shape 2+1
nodes.statement: \varphi'&=\varphi_{-N', u'}\oplus\lambda_{\varepsilon', t'}
nodes.label: E:2+1

nodes.name: Central character relation
nodes.statement: -(\varepsilon_1+\varepsilon_2+\varepsilon_3)+t_1+t_2+t_3=2u'-N'-\varepsilon'+t',
nodes.label: E:central

nodes.name: Twisted parameters
nodes.statement: Next note that for each $\lambda_{\delta, s}$ we have \begin{align*} \varphi\otimes\lambda_{\delta, s} &=\lambda_{\delta_1, t_1+s-\gamma_1}\oplus\lambda_{\delta_2, t_2+s-\gamma_2}\oplus \lambda_{\delta_3, t_3+s-\gamma_3}\\ \varphi'\otimes\lambda_{\delta,s} &=\varphi_{-N',u'+s-\delta}\oplus\lambda_{\delta', t'+s-\gamma'} \end{align*} where $\delta_i=\varepsilon_i+\delta\pmod{2}$ and $\gamma_i=2$ (resp.\ 0) if $\varepsilon_i=\delta=1$ (resp.\ otherwise), and similarly for $\delta'$ and $\gamma'$.
nodes.statement_short: Compute the twists by $\lambda_{\delta,s}$.

nodes.name: Multiset identity for GL(3)
nodes.statement: \{t_1-\gamma_1, t_2-\gamma_2, t_3-\gamma_3\} =\{u'-\delta, u'-\delta+1, t'-\gamma'\}
nodes.label: E:multisets_GL(3)

nodes.name: Multiset identity after reordering
nodes.statement: \{t_1-\gamma_1, t_1+1-\gamma_2, t_3-\gamma_3\} =\{t_1-\delta, t_1+1-\delta, t_3-\gamma'\}.
nodes.label: E:multisets_GL(3)-1

nodes.name: Parity condition from central character
nodes.statement: \varepsilon_1+\varepsilon_2+\varepsilon_3-\varepsilon'>1.
nodes.label: E:epsilon

nodes.name: t_1-gamma_1 not minimal
nodes.statement: Assume $t_1-\gamma_1$ is a minimal element in the left hand side . Then we must have $\gamma_1=2$ (so $\varepsilon_1=1$), because $t_1-1$ is in the left hand side and so we must have $t_1-\gamma_1\preceq t_1-1$, and hence we have \[ \{t_1-2, t_1+1-\gamma_2, t_3-\gamma_3\} =\{t_1-1, t_1, t_3-\gamma'\}. \] Then we must have $t_1-2=t_3-\gamma'$, which implies \[ \{t_1+1-\gamma_2, t_1-2-\gamma_3+\gamma'\} =\{t_1-1, t_1\}. \] Considering $1-\gamma_2$ is always odd, we conclude $t_1+1-\gamma_2=t_1-1$, which implies $\gamma_2=2$ (so $\varepsilon_2=1$), and $t_1-2-\gamma_3+\gamma'=t_1$, which implies $\gamma_3=0$ (so $\varepsilon_3=0$) and $\gamma'=2$ (so $\varepsilon'=1$). But this contradicts the condition \eqref{E:epsilon} coming from the central character assumption. Hence $t_1-\gamma_1$ cannot be minimal in the left hand side of \eqref{E:multisets_GL(3)-2}.
nodes.statement_short: Minimality of $t_1-\gamma_1$ contradicts (6.6).

nodes.name: t_1+1-gamma_2 not minimal
nodes.statement: Suppose now that $t_1+1-\gamma_2$ is minimal. Then this implies that $\gamma_1=0$ and $\gamma_2=2$, in which case $\varepsilon_1=0$ and $\varepsilon_2=1$. Then \eqref{E:multisets_GL(3)-2} implies $t_3-\gamma_3=t_3-\gamma'$, which implies $\gamma_3=\gamma'$, which in turn implies $\varepsilon_3=\varepsilon'$. Then the left hand side of \eqref{E:epsilon} will be $1$, which is a contradiction. Hence neither $t_1-\gamma_1$ nor $t_2+1-\gamma_2$ can be minimal.
nodes.statement_short: Minimality of $t_1+1-\gamma_2$ also contradicts (6.6).

nodes.name: t_3-gamma_3 minimal impossible
nodes.statement: So $t_3-\gamma_3$ can be the only minimal element, which means \[ t_3-\gamma_3\prec t_1-1\prec t_1 \] or \[ t_3-\gamma_3\prec t_1-2\prec t_1+1-\gamma_2. \] The first case comes from the situation where $\gamma_1 = 0, \gamma_2 = 2$, which we argued earlier cannot happen. We consider the second case. Notice that all the elements are comparable and the inequalities are all strict. Hence the same has to happen in the right hand side. But one can easily see that this is impossible because the right hand side already contains $t_1-1$ and $t_1$ while the second largest element in the left hand side is $t_1-2$.
nodes.statement_short: The remaining case contradicts the shape of the right side.

nodes.name: Mixed shapes excluded
nodes.statement: Hence we conclude that we cannot have both \eqref{E:1+1+1} and \eqref{E:2+1} at the same time; namely, if $\varphi$ is a sum of three irreducible representations, so is $\varphi'$, and if $\varphi$ is a sum of two irreducible representations, so is $\varphi'$.
nodes.statement_short: Both parameters have the same shape.

nodes.name: Case: three characters each
nodes.statement: First, assume \begin{align*} \varphi&=\lambda_{\varepsilon_1, t_1}\oplus\lambda_{\varepsilon_2, t_2}\oplus\lambda_{\varepsilon_3, t_3}\\ \varphi'&=\lambda_{\varepsilon'_1, t'_1}\oplus\lambda_{\varepsilon'_2, t'_2}\oplus\lambda_{\varepsilon'_3, t'_3}. \end{align*} Then the argument is similar to Step 2 of the real case. Namely by twisting by $\lambda_{0, s}$ and equating the $L$-factors, one can get \[ \{t_1,t_2,t_3\}=\{t'_1,t'_2,t'_3\} \] as multisets. Also by twisting by $\lambda_{1,s}$ and equating the $L$-factors, one can get \[ \{t_1-\gamma_1,t_2-\gamma_2,t_3-\gamma_3\}= \{t'_1-\gamma'_1,t'_2-\gamma'_2,t'_3-\gamma'_3\} \] as multisets, where $\gamma_i=2$ if $\varepsilon_i=1$, and $\gamma_i=0$ if $\varepsilon_i=0$, and similarly for $\gamma'_i$. Then the argument of Step 2 of the real case goes through with the $\varepsilon$'s replaced by $\gamma$'s. Hence we get $\varphi=\varphi'$.
nodes.statement_short: Twists by $\lambda_{0,s}$ and $\lambda_{1,s}$ and the argument of real Step 2 give $\varphi=\varphi'$.

nodes.name: Case: 2+1 each
nodes.statement: Next, assume \begin{align*} \varphi&=\varphi_{-N, t}\oplus\lambda_{\varepsilon, u}\\ \varphi'&=\varphi_{-N', t'}\oplus\lambda_{\varepsilon', u'}. \end{align*} By twisting $\lambda_{\delta, s}$, equating the $L$-factors and using the duplication formula, one obtains \[ \{t-\delta, t+1-\delta, u-\gamma\}= \{t'-\delta, t'+1-\delta, u'-\gamma'\} \] where $\gamma=2$ if $\varepsilon=\delta=1$ and 0 otherwise, and similarly for $\gamma'$. By examining minimal elements, one can see that this implies $t=t'$, $u=u'$ and $\gamma=\gamma'$ (so $\varepsilon=\varepsilon'$). (The detail is left to the reader.) Finally the central character assumption implies $N=N'$. The proposition follows.
nodes.statement_short: Minimal-element comparison gives $t=t'$, $u=u'$, $\varepsilon=\varepsilon'$; central character gives $N=N'$.

nodes.name: Central character assumption necessary for n=2
nodes.statement: Let us remark that even when $n=2$, the assumption on the central character is necessary.
conclusions: the assumption on the central character is necessary

nodes.name: GL_2(R) parameters not distinguished by GL(1)-twists
nodes.statement: Let \begin{align*} \varphi&=\varphi_{-N, t}\\ \varphi'&=\varphi_{-N', t} \end{align*} with $N>0, N'>0$ but $N\neq N'$. Then for any $\lambda_{\delta, s}$, we have \[ L(\varphi\otimes\lambda_{\delta, s})=L(\varphi'\otimes\lambda_{\delta,s}) =2(2\pi)^{-(t+s-\delta)}\Gamma(t+s-\delta). \] Of course, there are infinitely many such choices for $N$ and $N'$. If we further assume $N=N'\pmod{4}$, not only the $L$-factors but the $\epsilon$-factors coincide. Indeed, we can compute \[ \epsilon(\varphi\otimes\lambda_{\delta, s}, \psi_{\mathbb{R}})=\epsilon(\varphi'\otimes\lambda_{\delta, s}, \psi_{\mathbb{R}}) =-i^{N+1}=-i^{N'+1}, \] and again there are infinitely many such choices.
nodes.statement_short: $\varphi_{-N,t}$ and $\varphi_{-N',t}$ with $N\ne N'$ have equal $\operatorname{GL}(1)$-twisted $L$-factors (and $\epsilon$-factors if $N\equiv N'$ mod 4).

nodes.name: GL(2)-twists needed for GL_4(R)
nodes.statement: Finally, the following example for $\operatorname{GL}_4(\mathbb{R})$ shows that, even with the central character assumption and the equality of the $\epsilon$-factors, one will still need $\operatorname{GL}(2)$-twists.
assumptions: even with the central character assumption and the equality of the $\epsilon$-factors

nodes.name: GL_4(R) family indistinguishable by GL(1)-twists
nodes.statement: Let \begin{align*} \varphi&=\varphi_{-N_1, t_1}\oplus\varphi_{-N_2, t_2}\\ \varphi'&=\varphi_{-N'_1, t'_1}\oplus\varphi_{-N'_2, t'_2}. \end{align*} Let $\omega$ and $\omega'$ be the central characters of the representations corresponding to $\varphi$ and $\varphi'$, respectively. Then by \eqref{E:central_character} we know \begin{align*} \omega(r)&=r^{-(N_1+N_2)+2(t_1+t_2)}\\ \omega'(r)&=r^{-(N'_1+N'_2)+2(t'_1+t'_2)} \end{align*} for $r\in\mathbb{R}^\times$. For each $\lambda_{\delta, s}$, we have \begin{align*} L(\varphi\otimes\lambda_{\delta,s})&=4(2\pi)^{-(2s+t_1+t_2-2\delta)} \Gamma(s+t_1-\delta)\Gamma(s+t_2-\delta)\\ L(\varphi'\otimes\lambda_{\delta,s})&=4(2\pi)^{-(2s+t'_1+t'_2-2\delta)} \Gamma(s+t'_1-\delta)\Gamma(s+t'_2-\delta) \end{align*} and \begin{align*} \epsilon(\varphi\otimes\lambda_{\delta,s}, \psi_{\mathbb{R}})&=i^{N_1+N_2+2}\\ \epsilon(\varphi'\otimes\lambda_{\delta,s}, \psi_{\mathbb{R}})&=i^{N'_1+N'_2+2}. \end{align*} Hence if we have \[ N_1+N_2=N'_1+N'_2\quad\text{and}\quad \{t_1, t_2\}=\{t'_1, t'_2\}, \] then the $L$-factors, $\epsilon$-factors and central characters will all coincide. Of course there are infinitely many such choices.
nodes.statement_short: Sums of two $\varphi_{-N_i,t_i}$ with equal $N_1+N_2$ and $\{t_1,t_2\}$ share $L$-, $\epsilon$-factors and central character under $\operatorname{GL}(1)$-twists.

nodes.name: Proof that F^x is the abelianized Weil group
nodes.statement: This is obvious if $F=\mathbb C$. If $F=\mathbb{R}$, we have a surjective map \begin{equation} W_{\mathbb{R}}\longrightarrow \mathbb{R}^\times, \quad z\mapsto z\bar{z},\; j\mapsto -1, \end{equation} whose kernel is the commutator group $[W_{\mathbb{R}}, W_{\mathbb{R}}]$, which is actually of the form $\{z\in\mathbb C^\times:|z|=1\}$.
nodes.statement_short: Trivial for $\mathbb C$; for $\mathbb R$ use the norm map $W_{\mathbb R}\to\mathbb R^\times$, whose kernel is the commutator subgroup.

nodes.name: General Langlands parameter over C
nodes.statement: Then in general, an $n$-dimensional representation $\varphi:W_{\mathbb C}\rightarrow\operatorname{GL}_n(\mathbb C)$ is of the form \begin{equation} \varphi=\chi_{-N_1,t_1}\oplus\cdots\oplus\chi_{-N_n, t_n}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Every $n$-dimensional representation of $W_{\mathbb C}$ is a sum of $n$ characters $\chi_{-N_i,t_i}$.

nodes.name: Determinant of phi_{-N,t}
nodes.statement: Hence from \eqref{E:W_R}, as a character on $\mathbb{R}^\times$ we can identify $\det(\varphi_{-N,t})$ with $\operatorname{sign}\chi_{-N, t}$ where $\chi_{-N, t}$ is viewed as a character on $\mathbb{R}^\times$ via the inclusion $\mathbb{R}^\times\subseteq\mathbb C^\times$. Namely \begin{equation} r\mapsto\operatorname{sign}(r) r^{-N}|r|^{2t}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: $\det\varphi_{-N,t}$ is the character $r\mapsto\operatorname{sign}(r)r^{-N}|r|^{2t}$ of $\mathbb R^\times$.

nodes.name: phi_{-N,t} = phi_{N,t-N}
nodes.statement: Also since $\operatorname{Ind}_{W_{\mathbb C}}^{W_{\mathbb{R}}}\chi_{-N,t}=\operatorname{Ind}_{W_{\mathbb C}}^{W_{\mathbb{R}}}\overline{\chi_{-N,t}}$, we have \begin{equation} \varphi_{-N,t}=\varphi_{N, t-N}. \end{equation}

nodes.name: General Langlands parameter over R
nodes.statement: In general, an $n$-dimensional representation $\varphi:W_{\mathbb{R}}\rightarrow\operatorname{GL}_n(\mathbb C)$ is of the form \begin{equation} \varphi=\left(\lambda_{\varepsilon_1,t_1}\oplus\cdots\oplus\lambda_{\varepsilon_p,t_p}\right)\oplus \left(\varphi_{-N_1,u_1}\oplus\cdots\oplus\varphi_{-N_q, u_q}\right) \end{equation} where $N_i>0$ for all $i$, and $p+2q=n$.
nodes.statement_short: Every $n$-dim representation of $W_{\mathbb R}$ is a sum of $p$ characters $\lambda$ and $q$ irreducible $\varphi_{-N_i,u_i}$, $p+2q=n$.

nodes.name: L- and epsilon-factors of chi_{-N,t}
nodes.statement: Assume $F=\mathbb C$. Then the $L$- and $\epsilon$-factors of the character $\chi_{-N,t}$ are defined as \begin{align} \notag L(\chi_{-N, t})&=2(2\pi)^{-(t-\frac{N}{2}+\frac{|N|}{2})}\Gamma(t-\frac{N}{2}+\frac{|N|}{2})\\ &=\begin{cases}2(2\pi)^{-t}\Gamma(t),\quad\text{if $N\geq 0$};\\ 2(2\pi)^{-(t-N)}\Gamma(t-N),\quad\text{if $N<0$}, \end{cases}\\ \epsilon(\chi_{-N,t},\psi_{\mathbb C})&=i^{|N|}. \end{align}

nodes.name: L- and epsilon-factors of lambda_{epsilon,t}
nodes.statement: Assume $F=\mathbb{R}$. For the 1-dimensional $\lambda_{\varepsilon, t}$, \begin{align} L(\lambda_{\varepsilon,t})&=\pi^{-\frac{t}{2}}\Gamma\left(\frac{t}{2}\right),\\ \epsilon(\lambda_{\varepsilon,t},\psi_{\mathbb{R}})&=(-i)^\varepsilon. \end{align}

nodes.name: L- and epsilon-factors of phi_{-N,t}
nodes.statement: For the 2-dimensional representation $\varphi_{-N,t}$, \begin{align} L(\varphi_{-N,t})&=L(\chi_{-N,t}) =\begin{cases}2(2\pi)^{-t}\Gamma(t),\quad\text{if $N\geq 0$};\\ 2(2\pi)^{-(t-N)}\Gamma(t-N),\quad\text{if $N<0$}, \end{cases}\\ \epsilon(\varphi_{-N,t},\psi_{\mathbb{R}})&=-i\cdot\epsilon(\chi_{-N,t},\psi_{\mathbb C})=-i^{|N|+1}. \end{align}

nodes.name: GL(1)-twist of a parameter over C
nodes.statement: Assume $F=\mathbb C$. Let $\chi_{-M,s}$ be a character on $\mathbb C^\times$, and let $\varphi$ be an $n$-dimensional representation of $W_{\mathbb C}$ as in \eqref{E:general_parameter_C}. Then the twist $\varphi\otimes\chi_{-M,s}$ by $\chi_{-M,s}$ is given by \begin{equation} \varphi\otimes\chi_{-M,s} =\chi_{-(N_1+M), t_1+s}\oplus\cdots\oplus\chi_{-(N_n+M), t_n+s}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Twisting $\varphi=\oplus\chi_{-N_i,t_i}$ by $\chi_{-M,s}$ shifts each summand to $\chi_{-(N_i+M),t_i+s}$.
assumptions: $\varphi$ be an $n$-dimensional representation of $W_{\mathbb C}$ as in \eqref{E:general_parameter_C}
conclusions: the twist $\varphi\otimes\chi_{-M,s}$ by $\chi_{-M,s}$ is given by

nodes.name: Local factors of phi_{-N,t} twisted by lambda
nodes.statement: Accordingly, we have \begin{align} L(\varphi_{-N, t}\otimes\lambda_{\delta, s})&=\begin{cases} 2(2\pi)^{-(t+s-\delta)}\Gamma(t+s-\delta),\quad\text{if $N\geq 0$};\\ 2(2\pi)^{-(t+s-\delta-N)}\Gamma(t+s-\delta-N) \quad\text{if $N<0$}; \end{cases}\\ \epsilon(\varphi_{-N, t}\otimes\lambda_{\delta, s}, \psi_{\mathbb{R}})&=-i^{|N|+1}. \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Explicit $L$- and $\epsilon$-factors of $\varphi_{-N,t}\otimes\lambda_{\delta,s}$.

nodes.name: Local factors of GL(2) x GL(2) twist
nodes.statement: Then, coupled together with the identity \[ \varphi_{-(N-M), t+s-M}=\varphi_{-(M-N), t+s-N} \] (by \eqref{E:N>0}), we obtain \begin{align} L(\varphi_{-N,t}\otimes\varphi_{-M,s})&=4(2\pi)^{-2(t+s)+\min\{N, M\}}\cdot\Gamma(t+s)\cdot \Gamma(t+s-\min\{N, M\})\\ \epsilon(\varphi_{-N,t}\otimes\varphi_{-M,s})&=(-1)^{\max\{N, M\}}. \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: $L(\varphi_{-N,t}\otimes\varphi_{-M,s})=4(2\pi)^{\dots}\Gamma(t+s)\Gamma(t+s-\min\{N,M\})$ and $\epsilon=(-1)^{\max\{N,M\}}$.

nodes.name: Gamma-product comparison lemma
nodes.statement: Let $t_1,\dots, t_m, t'_1,\dots, t'_{m'}\in\mathbb C$. Suppose \begin{equation} F(s)\cdot\prod_{i=1}^m\Gamma(s+t_i)=\prod_{j=1}^{m'}\Gamma(s+t'_j) \end{equation} as functions in $s$, where $F(s)$ is a function on $\mathbb C$ whose zeros and poles do not interfere with the poles of the $\Gamma(s+t_i)$'s and $\Gamma(s+t'_i)$'s. Then $m=m'$, and further for each $i\in\{1,\dots,m\}$, there is a corresponding $j\in\{1,\dots,m'\}$ such that $t_i=t'_j$, namely \[ \{t_1,\dots,t_m\}=\{t'_1,\dots,t'_{m'}\} \] as multisets. Accordingly, $F\equiv 1$.
nodes.statement_short: If $F(s)\prod\Gamma(s+t_i)=\prod\Gamma(s+t'_j)$ with $F$ harmless, then the multisets $\{t_i\}$ and $\{t'_j\}$ agree and $F\equiv1$.
assumptions: $F(s)$ is a function on $\mathbb C$ whose zeros and poles do not interfere with the poles of the $\Gamma(s+t_i)$'s and $\Gamma(s+t'_i)$'s
nodes.label: L:Lemma

nodes.name: Proof of the local converse theorem for GL_n(C)
nodes.statement:
We will prove our main theorem for $F=\mathbb C$. Let $\pi$ and $\pi'$ be infinitesimal equivalence classes of irreducible admissible representations of $\operatorname{GL}_n(\mathbb C)$, and assume that their corresponding Langlands parameters $\varphi$ and $\varphi'$ are given by  egin{align*} \varphi&=\chi_{-N_1,t_1}\oplus\cdots\oplus\chi_{-N_n, t_n}\ \varphi'&=\chi_{-N'_1,t'_1}\oplus\cdots\oplus\chi_{-N'_n, t'_n}. \end{align*} The assertion $L(s, \pi	imes	au)=L(s, \pi'	imes	au)$ for all $	au\in\operatorname{Irr}_1$ is the same as  egin{equation} L(\varphi\otimes\chi_{-M, s})=L(\varphi'\otimes\chi_{-M, s}) \end{equation} for all $M\in\mathbb{Z}$ and $s\in\mathbb C$. As in \eqref{E:twisted_general_parameter_C}, we have  egin{align*} \varphi\otimes\chi_{-M,s}&=\chi_{-(N_1+M),t_1+s}\oplus\cdots\oplus\chi_{-(N_n+M), t_n+s}\ \varphi'\otimes\chi_{-M,s}& =\chi_{-(N'_1+M),t'_1+s}\oplus\cdots\oplus\chi_{-(N'_n+M),t'_n+s}, \end{align*} and hence the equality \eqref{E:L-equality-C0} implies  egin{equation} \prod_{i=1}^nL(\chi_{-(N_i+M),t_i+s}) =\prod_{j=1}^nL(\chi_{-(N'_j+M),t'_j+s}) \end{equation} for all $M\in\mathbb{Z}$ and $s\in\mathbb C$. We will show \eqref{E:L-equality-C} implies $\varphi=\varphi'$. But once we show that $\varphi$ and $\varphi'$ have a common constituent, the theorem follows by induction. Namely, it suffices to prove  egin{equation} \chi_{-N_i, t_i}=\chi_{-N'_j, t'_j} \end{equation} for some $i, j\in\{1,\dots,n\}$. The basic idea of our proof is that we will examine ``maximal poles'' of both sides of \eqref{E:L-equality-C} for different choices of $M$. Our proof has three major steps, which is outlined as follows. In Step 1, we will show that $\{t_1,\dots, t_n\}=\{t'_1,\dots, t'_n\}$ as multisets. In Step 2, we will show that $\min\{N_1,\dots,N_n\}=\min\{N'_1,\dots,N'_n\}$. Finally in Step 3, we will finish up the proof of the theorem. In each of the steps we will choose an appropriate $M$. \subsection{Step 1} Let us choose $M$ large enough so that $N_i+M> 0$ and $N'_j+M>0$ for all $i, j\in\{1,\cdots,n\}$. By \eqref{E:L-factor-C}, we can write \eqref{E:L-equality-C} as \[ F(s)\prod_{i=1}^n\Gamma(s+t_i)=\prod_{j=1}^n\Gamma(s+t'_j) \] for some function $F(s)$ without a pole or zero. Hence by Lemma ef{L:Lemma}, we have \[ \{t_1,\dots, t_n\}=\{t'_1,\dots, t'_n\} \] as multisets. \subsection{Step 2} Let us first note that we can now reorder the indices $i$ and $j$ in such a way that  egin{equation} t_1=t'_1, t_2=t'_2,\dots, t_n=t'_n. \end{equation} Let  egin{align*} N_{\min}:=&\min\{N_1,\dots,N_n\}\ N'_{\min}:=&\min\{N'_1,\dots,N'_n\}. \end{align*} As we mentioned above, we will show $N_{\min}=N'_{\min}$ in this step. First assume $N'_{\min}<N_{\min}$. Choose $M=-N'_{\min}-1$. Then \eqref{E:L-equality-C} is written as  egin{equation} F(s)\prod_{i=1}^n\Gamma(s+t_i)=\prod_{j=1}^n\Gamma(s+t'_j+\varepsilon_j), \end{equation} where \[ \varepsilon_j= egin{cases}1,\quad	ext{if $N'_j=N'_{\min}$};\ 0,\quad	ext{if $N'_j>N'_{\min}$}, \end{cases} \] and $\varepsilon_j
eq 0$ for at least one $j$. Now the left hand side of \eqref{E:L-equality-C1} has a maximal pole at $s=-t_k$ for some $t_k$ which is minimal in $\{t_1,\dots,t_n\}$. Then $t_k=t'_l+\varepsilon_l$ for some $l$ and $t'_l+\varepsilon_l$ is minimal in $\{t'_1+\varepsilon_1,\dots,t'_n+\varepsilon_n\}$. Assume $\varepsilon_l=1$. Then we have $t'_l+\varepsilon_l=t_l+1$ by \eqref{E:relation2}, which implies $t_l+1=t_k$. But then $t_l\prec t_k$, which contradicts the minimality of $t_k$. Hence $\varepsilon_l=0$, namely $t_k=t'_l$. Then \eqref{E:L-equality-C1} is now written as  egin{equation} F(s)\prod_{i
eq k}\Gamma(s+t_i)=\prod_{j
eq l}\Gamma(s+t'_j+\varepsilon_j). \end{equation} by cancelling $\Gamma (s+t_k)$ from the left and $\Gamma (s+t'_l)$ from the right. By arguing inductively, one can show that $\varepsilon_j=0$ for all $j\in\{1,\dots,n\}$ which is a contradiction. Hence we must have $N'_{\min}\geq N_{\min}$. By symmetry, we can show that $N'_{\min}\leq N_{\min}$. Hence $N_{\min}=N'_{\min}$. \subsection{Step 3} Finally, we will show \eqref{E:goal} for some $i$ and $j$, which will complete the proof of the theorem. For this purpose, let us reorder the indices so that  egin{equation} N_1=N_2=\cdots=N_d<N_{d+1}\leq\cdots\leq N_n, \end{equation} while still keeping the relation \eqref{E:relation2}. Such indexing is certainly possible. Now let us twist $\varphi$ and $\varphi'$ by $\chi_{-M,s}$ with $M=-N_1-1=-N'_{\min}-1$. Then \eqref{E:L-equality-C} is now written as  egin{equation} F(s)\prod_{i=1}^d\Gamma(s+t_i+1)\cdot\prod_{i=d+1}^n\Gamma(s+t_i) =\prod_{j=1}^n\Gamma(s+t'_j+\varepsilon_j) \end{equation} where $\varepsilon_j$ is as before and $\varepsilon_j=1$ for at least one $j$. Let  egin{align*} A&:=A_1\cup A_2, \quad A_1:=\{t_i+1:i\in\{1,\dots,d\}\},\quad A_2:=\{t_i:i\in\{d+1,\dots,n\}\}\ B&:=\{t'_j+\varepsilon_j: j\in\{1,\dots,n\}\}. \end{align*} Of course by Lemma ef{L:Lemma}, we know $A=B$ as multisets. We will again look at ``maximal poles'' of \eqref{E:L-equality-C3}, which correspond to minimal elements of $A=B$. We consider the following two cases, depending on whether a minimal element is in $A_1$ or $A_2$. First assume $t_k+1\in A_1$ with $k\leq d$ is minmal in $A$. By $A=B$, we have $t_k+1=t'_l+\varepsilon_l$ for some $l$, which is minimal in $B$. Assume $\varepsilon_l=1$. Then this means $N'_l=N_1=N_k$ and $t_k=t'_l$. Hence we have \eqref{E:goal} with $i=k$ and $j=l$. Assume $\varepsilon_l=0$. First assume $\varepsilon_k=0$. Then $t'_k+\varepsilon_k=t_k=t'_l+\varepsilon_l-1$, namely $t'_k+\varepsilon_k\prec t'_l+\varepsilon_l$, which contradicts the minimality of $t'_l+\varepsilon_l$. Hence $\varepsilon_k=1$, which implies $N'_k=N_1=N_k$. Since $t_k=t'_k$ by \eqref{E:relation2}, the equality \eqref{E:goal} is satisfied with $i=j=k$. Next assume that $t_k\in A_2$ with $k>d$ is minmal in $A$. By $A=B$, we know that $t_k=t'_l+\varepsilon_l$ for some $l$, which is minimal in $B$. Assume $\varepsilon_l=1$, so $t_k=t'_l+1=t_l+1$. Then $t_l\prec t_k$. Since $t_k$ is minimal in $A$, we must have $l\leq d$. Hence $N_l=N_1$. Also since $\varepsilon_l=1$ implies $N'_l=N_1$, we have $N'_l=N_l$. Hence, we have \eqref{E:goal} with $i=j=l$. Finally assume $\varepsilon_l=0$, 	ext{i.e.\ } $t_k=t'_l$. Then we can reorder the indices $j$ for the multiset $B$ by swapping $k$ and $l$ without changing the relations \eqref{E:relation2} and \eqref{E:relation1}. So we can cancel $\Gamma(s+t_k)$ from both sides of \eqref{E:L-equality-C3}. We can now argue inductively by repeating the above arguments until we obtain \eqref{E:goal}. The proof is complete.
nodes.statement_short: Compare maximal poles of twisted $L$-factors (Lemma 3.1) for suitable $\chi_{-M,s}$, find a common constituent, and induct. Three steps: equal $t$-multisets, equal $\min N$, then a common character.

nodes.name: Setup and reduction
nodes.statement: We will prove our main theorem for $F=\mathbb C$. Let $\pi$ and $\pi'$ be infinitesimal equivalence classes of irreducible admissible representations of $\operatorname{GL}_n(\mathbb C)$, and assume that their corresponding Langlands parameters $\varphi$ and $\varphi'$ are given by \begin{align*} \varphi&=\chi_{-N_1,t_1}\oplus\cdots\oplus\chi_{-N_n, t_n}\\ \varphi'&=\chi_{-N'_1,t'_1}\oplus\cdots\oplus\chi_{-N'_n, t'_n}. \end{align*} The assertion $L(s, \pi\times\tau)=L(s, \pi'\times\tau)$ for all $\tau\in\operatorname{Irr}_1$ is the same as \begin{equation} L(\varphi\otimes\chi_{-M, s})=L(\varphi'\otimes\chi_{-M, s}) \end{equation} for all $M\in\mathbb{Z}$ and $s\in\mathbb C$. As in \eqref{E:twisted_general_parameter_C}, we have \begin{align*} \varphi\otimes\chi_{-M,s}&=\chi_{-(N_1+M),t_1+s}\oplus\cdots\oplus\chi_{-(N_n+M), t_n+s}\\ \varphi'\otimes\chi_{-M,s}& =\chi_{-(N'_1+M),t'_1+s}\oplus\cdots\oplus\chi_{-(N'_n+M),t'_n+s}, \end{align*} and hence the equality \eqref{E:L-equality-C0} implies \begin{equation} \prod_{i=1}^nL(\chi_{-(N_i+M),t_i+s}) =\prod_{j=1}^nL(\chi_{-(N'_j+M),t'_j+s}) \end{equation} for all $M\in\mathbb{Z}$ and $s\in\mathbb C$. We will show \eqref{E:L-equality-C} implies $\varphi=\varphi'$. But once we show that $\varphi$ and $\varphi'$ have a common constituent, the theorem follows by induction. Namely, it suffices to prove \begin{equation} \chi_{-N_i, t_i}=\chi_{-N'_j, t'_j} \end{equation} for some $i, j\in\{1,\dots,n\}$. The basic idea of our proof is that we will examine ``maximal poles'' of both sides of \eqref{E:L-equality-C} for different choices of $M$. Our proof has three major steps, which is outlined as follows. In Step 1, we will show that $\{t_1,\dots, t_n\}=\{t'_1,\dots, t'_n\}$ as multisets. In Step 2, we will show that $\min\{N_1,\dots,N_n\}=\min\{N'_1,\dots,N'_n\}$. Finally in Step 3, we will finish up the proof of the theorem. In each of the steps we will choose an appropriate $M$.
nodes.statement_short: Translate to Langlands parameters and reduce to finding one common constituent.

nodes.name: Rewrite twisted L-equality
nodes.statement: The assertion $L(s, \pi\times\tau)=L(s, \pi'\times\tau)$ for all $\tau\in\operatorname{Irr}_1$ is the same as \begin{equation} L(\varphi\otimes\chi_{-M, s})=L(\varphi'\otimes\chi_{-M, s}) \end{equation} for all $M\in\mathbb{Z}$ and $s\in\mathbb C$.
nodes.statement_short: The hypothesis becomes equality (4.2) of products of $L$-factors of characters.

nodes.name: Reduce to a common constituent
nodes.statement: We will show \eqref{E:L-equality-C} implies $\varphi=\varphi'$. But once we show that $\varphi$ and $\varphi'$ have a common constituent, the theorem follows by induction. Namely, it suffices to prove \begin{equation} \chi_{-N_i, t_i}=\chi_{-N'_j, t'_j} \end{equation} for some $i, j\in\{1,\dots,n\}$.
nodes.statement_short: By induction it suffices to find one common constituent (4.3).

nodes.name: Step 2: equal minimal N
nodes.statement:
\subsection{Step 2} Let us first note that we can now reorder the indices $i$ and $j$ in such a way that  egin{equation} t_1=t'_1, t_2=t'_2,\dots, t_n=t'_n. \end{equation} Let  egin{align*} N_{\min}:=&\min\{N_1,\dots,N_n\}\ N'_{\min}:=&\min\{N'_1,\dots,N'_n\}. \end{align*} As we mentioned above, we will show $N_{\min}=N'_{\min}$ in this step. First assume $N'_{\min}<N_{\min}$. Choose $M=-N'_{\min}-1$. Then \eqref{E:L-equality-C} is written as  egin{equation} F(s)\prod_{i=1}^n\Gamma(s+t_i)=\prod_{j=1}^n\Gamma(s+t'_j+\varepsilon_j), \end{equation} where \[ \varepsilon_j= egin{cases}1,\quad	ext{if $N'_j=N'_{\min}$};\ 0,\quad	ext{if $N'_j>N'_{\min}$}, \end{cases} \] and $\varepsilon_j
eq 0$ for at least one $j$. Now the left hand side of \eqref{E:L-equality-C1} has a maximal pole at $s=-t_k$ for some $t_k$ which is minimal in $\{t_1,\dots,t_n\}$. Then $t_k=t'_l+\varepsilon_l$ for some $l$ and $t'_l+\varepsilon_l$ is minimal in $\{t'_1+\varepsilon_1,\dots,t'_n+\varepsilon_n\}$. Assume $\varepsilon_l=1$. Then we have $t'_l+\varepsilon_l=t_l+1$ by \eqref{E:relation2}, which implies $t_l+1=t_k$. But then $t_l\prec t_k$, which contradicts the minimality of $t_k$. Hence $\varepsilon_l=0$, namely $t_k=t'_l$. Then \eqref{E:L-equality-C1} is now written as  egin{equation} F(s)\prod_{i
eq k}\Gamma(s+t_i)=\prod_{j
eq l}\Gamma(s+t'_j+\varepsilon_j). \end{equation} by cancelling $\Gamma (s+t_k)$ from the left and $\Gamma (s+t'_l)$ from the right. By arguing inductively, one can show that $\varepsilon_j=0$ for all $j\in\{1,\dots,n\}$ which is a contradiction. Hence we must have $N'_{\min}\geq N_{\min}$. By symmetry, we can show that $N'_{\min}\leq N_{\min}$. Hence $N_{\min}=N'_{\min}$.
nodes.statement_short: Show $N_{\min}=N'_{\min}$ by contradiction, twisting with $M=-N'_{\min}-1$.

nodes.name: Reorder and define minima
nodes.statement: Let us first note that we can now reorder the indices $i$ and $j$ in such a way that \begin{equation} t_1=t'_1, t_2=t'_2,\dots, t_n=t'_n. \end{equation} Let \begin{align*} N_{\min}:=&\min\{N_1,\dots,N_n\}\\ N'_{\min}:=&\min\{N'_1,\dots,N'_n\}. \end{align*} As we mentioned above, we will show $N_{\min}=N'_{\min}$ in this step.
nodes.statement_short: Align $t_i=t'_i$ and define $N_{\min},N'_{\min}$.

nodes.name: Assume N'_min < N_min and twist
nodes.statement: First assume $N'_{\min}<N_{\min}$. Choose $M=-N'_{\min}-1$. Then \eqref{E:L-equality-C} is written as \begin{equation} F(s)\prod_{i=1}^n\Gamma(s+t_i)=\prod_{j=1}^n\Gamma(s+t'_j+\varepsilon_j), \end{equation} where \[ \varepsilon_j=\begin{cases}1,\quad\text{if $N'_j=N'_{\min}$};\\ 0,\quad\text{if $N'_j>N'_{\min}$}, \end{cases} \] and $\varepsilon_j\neq 0$ for at least one $j$.
nodes.statement_short: Suppose $N'_{\min}<N_{\min}$; twisting by $M=-N'_{\min}-1$ gives (4.5).

nodes.name: Cancel matched factors
nodes.statement: Then \eqref{E:L-equality-C1} is now written as \begin{equation} F(s)\prod_{i\neq k}\Gamma(s+t_i)=\prod_{j\neq l}\Gamma(s+t'_j+\varepsilon_j). \end{equation} by cancelling $\Gamma (s+t_k)$ from the left and $\Gamma (s+t'_l)$ from the right.
nodes.statement_short: Cancel the matched gamma factors to get (4.6).

nodes.name: Step 3: find a common constituent
nodes.statement: \subsection{Step 3} Finally, we will show \eqref{E:goal} for some $i$ and $j$, which will complete the proof of the theorem. For this purpose, let us reorder the indices so that \begin{equation} N_1=N_2=\cdots=N_d<N_{d+1}\leq\cdots\leq N_n, \end{equation} while still keeping the relation \eqref{E:relation2}. Such indexing is certainly possible. Now let us twist $\varphi$ and $\varphi'$ by $\chi_{-M,s}$ with $M=-N_1-1=-N'_{\min}-1$. Then \eqref{E:L-equality-C} is now written as \begin{equation} F(s)\prod_{i=1}^d\Gamma(s+t_i+1)\cdot\prod_{i=d+1}^n\Gamma(s+t_i) =\prod_{j=1}^n\Gamma(s+t'_j+\varepsilon_j) \end{equation} where $\varepsilon_j$ is as before and $\varepsilon_j=1$ for at least one $j$. Let \begin{align*} A&:=A_1\cup A_2, \quad A_1:=\{t_i+1:i\in\{1,\dots,d\}\},\quad A_2:=\{t_i:i\in\{d+1,\dots,n\}\}\\ B&:=\{t'_j+\varepsilon_j: j\in\{1,\dots,n\}\}. \end{align*} Of course by Lemma \ref{L:Lemma}, we know $A=B$ as multisets. We will again look at ``maximal poles'' of \eqref{E:L-equality-C3}, which correspond to minimal elements of $A=B$. We consider the following two cases, depending on whether a minimal element is in $A_1$ or $A_2$. First assume $t_k+1\in A_1$ with $k\leq d$ is minmal in $A$. By $A=B$, we have $t_k+1=t'_l+\varepsilon_l$ for some $l$, which is minimal in $B$. Assume $\varepsilon_l=1$. Then this means $N'_l=N_1=N_k$ and $t_k=t'_l$. Hence we have \eqref{E:goal} with $i=k$ and $j=l$. Assume $\varepsilon_l=0$. First assume $\varepsilon_k=0$. Then $t'_k+\varepsilon_k=t_k=t'_l+\varepsilon_l-1$, namely $t'_k+\varepsilon_k\prec t'_l+\varepsilon_l$, which contradicts the minimality of $t'_l+\varepsilon_l$. Hence $\varepsilon_k=1$, which implies $N'_k=N_1=N_k$. Since $t_k=t'_k$ by \eqref{E:relation2}, the equality \eqref{E:goal} is satisfied with $i=j=k$. Next assume that $t_k\in A_2$ with $k>d$ is minmal in $A$. By $A=B$, we know that $t_k=t'_l+\varepsilon_l$ for some $l$, which is minimal in $B$. Assume $\varepsilon_l=1$, so $t_k=t'_l+1=t_l+1$. Then $t_l\prec t_k$. Since $t_k$ is minimal in $A$, we must have $l\leq d$. Hence $N_l=N_1$. Also since $\varepsilon_l=1$ implies $N'_l=N_1$, we have $N'_l=N_l$. Hence, we have \eqref{E:goal} with $i=j=l$. Finally assume $\varepsilon_l=0$, \text{i.e.\ } $t_k=t'_l$. Then we can reorder the indices $j$ for the multiset $B$ by swapping $k$ and $l$ without changing the relations \eqref{E:relation2} and \eqref{E:relation1}. So we can cancel $\Gamma(s+t_k)$ from both sides of \eqref{E:L-equality-C3}. We can now argue inductively by repeating the above arguments until we obtain \eqref{E:goal}. The proof is complete.
nodes.statement_short: Twist by $M=-N_1-1$ and compare minimal elements of $A=B$ in two cases to get (4.3).

nodes.name: Reorder by N
nodes.statement: Finally, we will show \eqref{E:goal} for some $i$ and $j$, which will complete the proof of the theorem. For this purpose, let us reorder the indices so that \begin{equation} N_1=N_2=\cdots=N_d<N_{d+1}\leq\cdots\leq N_n, \end{equation} while still keeping the relation \eqref{E:relation2}. Such indexing is certainly possible.
nodes.statement_short: Order indices so $N_1=\dots=N_d<N_{d+1}\le\dots$ keeping (4.4).

nodes.name: Twist by M=-N_1-1
nodes.statement: Now let us twist $\varphi$ and $\varphi'$ by $\chi_{-M,s}$ with $M=-N_1-1=-N'_{\min}-1$. Then \eqref{E:L-equality-C} is now written as \begin{equation} F(s)\prod_{i=1}^d\Gamma(s+t_i+1)\cdot\prod_{i=d+1}^n\Gamma(s+t_i) =\prod_{j=1}^n\Gamma(s+t'_j+\varepsilon_j) \end{equation} where $\varepsilon_j$ is as before and $\varepsilon_j=1$ for at least one $j$.
nodes.statement_short: Twisting gives the gamma identity (4.8).

nodes.name: Proof of the local converse theorem for GL_n(R)
nodes.statement:
We will prove our main theorem for $F=\mathbb{R}$. Assume $\pi, \pi'\in\operatorname{Irr}_n$ are such that $L(s, \pi	imes	au)=L(s,\pi'	imes	au)$ for all $	au\in\operatorname{Irr}_t$ with $t=1,2$. Namely if $\varphi$ and $\varphi'$ are the corresponding Langlands parameters, we have  egin{equation} L(\varphi\otimes\lambda_{\varepsilon,s})=L(\varphi'\otimes\lambda_{\varepsilon,s}) \end{equation} for all $\varepsilon\in\{0,1\}$ and $s\in\mathbb C$, and  egin{equation} L(\varphi\otimes\varphi_{-M,s})=L(\varphi'\otimes\varphi_{-M,s}) \end{equation} for all $M\in\mathbb{Z}$ and $s\in\mathbb C$. Let us write  egin{align*} \varphi&=\left(\lambda_{\varepsilon_1,t_1}\oplus\cdots\oplus\lambda_{\varepsilon_p,t_p}ight)\oplus \left(\varphi_{-N_1,u_1}\oplus\cdots\oplus\varphi_{-N_q, u_q}ight)\ \varphi'&=\left(\lambda_{\varepsilon'_1,t'_1}\oplus\cdots\oplus\lambda_{\varepsilon'_{p'},t'_{p'}}ight)\oplus \left(\varphi_{-N'_1,u'_1}\oplus\cdots\oplus\varphi_{-N'_{q'} u'_{q'}}ight) \end{align*} where we may assume $N_i>0$ and $N'_j>0$ for all $i, j$. Note that the numbers of 1-dimensional constituents for $\varphi$ and $\varphi'$ are, respectively, $p$ and $p'$, and those for 2-dimensional ones are, respectively, $q$ and $q'$, so $n=p+2q=p'+2q'$.\ The proof has three steps, and the basic philosophy is the same as the complex case in that we choose appropriate twists and examine ``maximal poles''. In Step 1, we will show $\{u_1, ..., u_q\}=\{u'_1, ..., u'_{q'} \}$ and $\{t_1-\varepsilon_1, ..., t_p-\varepsilon_p\}=\{t'_1-\varepsilon'_1, ..., t'_{p'}-\varepsilon'_{p'}\}$ as multisets, which also implies $p=p'$ and $q=q'$. In Step 2, we will show the 1-dimensional constituents are equal. Finally in Step 3, we will show the 2-dimensional constituents are equal. \subsection{Step 1} Consider the twist by $\varphi_{-M, s}$ with $M\geq 0$. Since all the $N_i$'s and $N'_j$'s are positive, \eqref{E:GL(2)xGL(1)_L} and \eqref{E:GL(2)xGL(2)_L} give  egin{align*} L(\varphi\otimes\varphi_{-M, s})&=F(s) \prod_{i=1}^{p}\Gamma(s+t_i-\varepsilon_i)\cdot \prod_{i=1}^{q}\Gamma(s+u_i)\cdot\Gamma(s+u_i-\min\{M, N_i\})\ L(\varphi'\otimes\varphi_{-M, s})&=F'(s) \prod_{j=1}^{p'}\Gamma(s+t'_j-\varepsilon'_j)\cdot \prod_{j=1}^{q'}\Gamma(s+u'_j)\cdot\Gamma(s+u'_j-\min\{M, N'_j\}), \end{align*} where $F(s)$ and $F'(s)$ are functions without a zero or pole. And the equality \eqref{E:GL(2)-twist} implies those two are equal. For the choices $M=0$ (so $\min\{M, N_i\} =\min\{M, N'_j\}=0$) and $M=1$ (so $\min\{M, N_i\} =\min\{M, N'_j\}=1$), Lemma ef{L:Lemma} implies  egin{align} &\{t_1-\varepsilon_1,\dots,t_p-\varepsilon_p\}\cup\{u_1,\dots,u_q\}\cup\{u_1,\dots,u_q\}\ 
otag=&\{t'_1-\varepsilon'_1,\dots,t'_{p'}-\varepsilon'_{p'}\}\cup\{u'_1,\dots,u'_{q'}\}\cup\{u'_1,\dots,u'_{q'}\}, \end{align} and  egin{align} &\{t_1-\varepsilon_1,\dots,t_p-\varepsilon_p\}\cup\{u_1,\dots,u_q\}\cup\{u_1-1,\dots,u_q-1\}\ 
otag=&\{t'_1-\varepsilon'_1,\dots,t'_{p'}-\varepsilon'_{p'}\}\cup\{u'_1,\dots,u'_{q'}\} \cup\{u'_1-1,\dots,u'_{q'}-1\} \end{align} as multisets. In what follows, by using \eqref{E:multisets_t_u-0} and \eqref{E:multisets_t_u-1}, we will show  egin{align} \{t_1-\varepsilon_1,\dots,t_p-\varepsilon_p\}&=\{t'_1-\varepsilon'_1,\dots,t'_{p'}-\varepsilon'_{p'}\}\ \{u_1,\dots,u_q\}&=\{u'_1,\dots,u'_{q'}\} \end{align} as multisets, which would also imply $p=p'$ and $q=q'$.
